chapters.title: Economy
paragraphs: When I wrote these pages, or most of them, I lived by myself in the woods, a mile from my nearest neighbor, in a house I had built with my own hands beside Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts. I supported myself entirely by manual labor. I stayed there for two years and two months. For now, I am once again a temporary resident of civilized life.

I would not press my personal affairs so insistently on my readers if my fellow townsmen had not asked such detailed questions about how I lived. Some would call their questions impertinent; to me, in the circumstances, they seem entirely natural and pertinent. Some asked what I ate, whether I felt lonely, whether I was afraid, and so on. Others wanted to know how much of my income went to charity; some with large families asked how many poor children I supported. Readers with no particular interest in me must therefore forgive me for attempting to answer a few of these questions here. Most books leave out the _I_, the first person; this book will keep it. As far as egotism goes, that is the main difference. We generally forget that, after all, it is always the first person speaking. I would talk less about myself if I knew anyone else equally well. Unfortunately, my limited experience confines me to this subject. For my part, I ask every writer, sooner or later, for a plain, honest account of his own life, rather than merely what he has heard about other people’s lives—something like the account he would send his family from a distant country. If he has lived honestly, it must have been in a country distant from mine. Perhaps these pages are addressed especially to poor students. Other readers can take whatever applies to them. I hope nobody will stretch the seams trying on this coat, for it may serve someone well whom it fits.

I would like to speak less about the Chinese and Sandwich Islanders than about you reading these pages, who are said to live in New England. I want to consider your condition, especially your outward circumstances here in this world and this town: what they are, whether they must be as bad as they are, and whether they could just as well be improved. I have traveled extensively in Concord, and everywhere—in shops, offices, and fields—the inhabitants seem to be doing penance in a thousand extraordinary ways. I have heard of Brahmins sitting among four fires and staring into the sun; hanging headfirst above flames; looking over their shoulders at the heavens “until it becomes impossible for them to resume their natural position, while from the twist of the neck nothing but liquids can pass into the stomach;” living chained for life at a tree’s foot; measuring great empires with their bodies like caterpillars; or balancing on one leg atop pillars. Even these deliberate penances are scarcely more astonishing or incredible than what I see daily. Hercules’ twelve labors were trifles beside those my neighbors undertake: there were only twelve, and they ended. I have never seen these men kill or capture a monster or finish a labor. They have no friend Iolas to sear the stump of the hydra’s head with a hot iron; crush one head and two spring up.

I see young fellow townsmen unfortunate enough to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farm equipment. These things are easier to acquire than to escape. Better if they had been born in an open pasture and suckled by a wolf: then they might see more clearly which field they were meant to work. Who turned them into serfs of the soil? Why must they eat their sixty acres when a man is sentenced to eat only his peck of dirt? Why start digging their graves at birth? They must live a human life while pushing all this before them, struggling along as best they can. How many poor immortal souls I have seen, nearly crushed and suffocated by their loads, crawling along life’s road! Before them they push a barn seventy-five feet long by forty wide, its Augean stables never cleaned, and a hundred acres of plowland, hayfield, pasture, and woodlot. Those without an inheritance, spared these needless inherited burdens, find enough work in mastering and cultivating a few cubic feet of flesh.

But people are laboring under a mistake. Before long, the better part of a man is plowed into the earth as compost. Under an apparent fate usually called necessity, they spend their lives, as an old book says, storing treasures that moth and rust destroy and thieves break in and steal. It is a fool’s life, as they will discover at its end, if not sooner. Deucalion and Pyrrha are said to have created people by throwing stones backward over their heads:—

Inde genus durum sumus, experiensque laborum,
Et documenta damus quâ simus origine nati.
Or, in Raleigh’s resonant rendering of it in rhyme,—

“From there our race is hard of heart, enduring pain and care,
Proving our bodies sprang from stone, and of its nature are.”
So much for blindly obeying a bungling oracle, tossing stones backward over their heads without seeing where the stones landed.

Even in this relatively free country, sheer ignorance and error keep most people so busy with artificial worries and unnecessarily coarse labor that life’s finer fruits remain beyond their reach. Overwork has made their fingers too clumsy and shaky to pick them. The working man actually has no leisure for real integrity in his daily life. He cannot afford the most fully human relations with others; his labor would lose value in the market. He has time to be nothing but a machine. How can someone who must constantly use his knowledge stay properly aware of his ignorance, as his growth requires? Before judging him, we ought sometimes to feed and clothe him free of charge and restore his strength with our cordials. The finest qualities in human nature, like the bloom on fruit, survive only the gentlest handling. Yet we show neither ourselves nor one another that tenderness.

We all know some of you are poor, struggling to live, sometimes almost gasping for breath. I do not doubt that some readers cannot pay for all the dinners they have eaten, or for coats and shoes rapidly wearing out or already worn through. You have reached this page to spend borrowed or stolen time, taking an hour from your creditors. Experience has sharpened my sight, and I can see plainly the mean, furtive lives many of you lead. Always on the edge, trying to get into business and out of debt—that ancient swamp the Latins called _æs alienum_, another’s brass, because some of their coins were brass—you live, die, and are buried on another’s brass. Always promising payment tomorrow, you die today insolvent. How many ways you seek favor and customers, stopping just short of offenses punishable by state prison! You lie, flatter, vote, shrink into a nutshell of politeness, or expand into an atmosphere of thin, misty generosity, all to persuade a neighbor to let you make his shoes, hat, coat, or carriage, or import his groceries. You make yourselves ill to put something aside for an illness: something hidden in an old chest or a stocking behind the plaster, or, more safely, in the brick bank. Anywhere will do, however much or little it may be.

Sometimes I wonder how we can be so frivolous, almost, as to concern ourselves with the gross but somewhat foreign bondage called Negro Slavery, when so many sharp and subtle masters enslave people both north and south. A southern overseer is hard to bear; a northern one is worse; but worst of all is driving yourself as your own slave. Talk of divinity in man! Look at the wagon driver traveling the highway to market by night or day. Does anything divine stir in him? His highest duty is feeding and watering his horses! What does his destiny matter to him beside the shipping interests? Is he not driving for Squire Make-a-stir? How godlike or immortal is he? Watch him cower and sneak, vaguely afraid all day, neither immortal nor divine, but enslaved and imprisoned by his own judgment of himself, a reputation earned through his own deeds. Public opinion is a feeble tyrant beside private opinion. What a man thinks of himself determines—or rather reveals—his fate. Who will be the Wilberforce to bring emancipation even to the West Indian provinces of imagination and fancy? Think, too, of the ladies weaving dressing-table cushions against the last day, careful not to betray too immature an interest in their destinies! As though time could be killed without wounding eternity.

Most people lead lives of quiet desperation. What passes for resignation is desperation firmly established. You leave the desperate city for the desperate countryside and must find consolation in the courage of minks and muskrats. Even humanity’s supposed games and amusements conceal a routine, unconscious despair. There is no real play in them, because play comes after work. Wisdom, however, is marked by its refusal to do desperate things.

When we consider humanity’s chief purpose, to borrow the catechism’s phrase, and the true necessities and means of living, it seems people must have deliberately chosen the usual way of life because they preferred it to every other. Yet they honestly believe no choice remains. Healthy, alert natures remember that the sun rose clear. We are never too old to abandon our prejudices. No habit of thought or action deserves trust without proof, however ancient it is. What everyone repeats, or silently accepts as true today, may prove false tomorrow: mere smoke of opinion mistaken for a cloud that would drop nourishing rain on their fields. Try what old people say you cannot do, and you discover you can. Old deeds suit old people, new deeds new ones. Once, perhaps, the old did not know enough to bring fresh fuel to keep a fire burning; the new put a little dry wood beneath a pot and fly around the globe as fast as birds, enough, as the phrase goes, to kill the old. Age is no better fitted to teach than youth—hardly as well—for it has lost more than it has gained. We might almost doubt whether the wisest person learns anything of absolute value through living. In practice the old have little important advice for the young. Their experience has been narrow, and their lives, for private reasons they must acknowledge, miserable failures. Perhaps some remaining faith contradicts that experience; perhaps they are merely less young than before. After some thirty years on this planet, I have yet to hear the first syllable of valuable, or even earnest, advice from my elders. They have told me nothing, and probably can tell me nothing useful. Here is life, an experiment largely untried by me; their having tried it does me no good. Whenever I think an experience valuable, I invariably reflect that my Mentors never mentioned it.

A farmer tells me, “You cannot live on vegetable food solely, for it furnishes nothing to make bones with.” Faithfully, then, he spends part of every day supplying his body with bone-making material. As he talks he walks behind his oxen, whose vegetable-built bones pull him and his cumbersome plow through every obstacle. Some things are actual necessities among certain people, the weakest and sickest, while elsewhere they are only luxuries, and elsewhere again entirely unknown.

Some people imagine their predecessors have explored all the terrain of human life, hills and valleys alike, and provided for everything. Evelyn says, “the wise Solomon prescribed ordinances for the very distances of trees; and the Roman prætors have decided how often you may go into your neighbor’s land to gather the acorns which fall on it without trespass, and what share belongs to that neighbor.” Even Hippocrates left instructions for trimming our nails: level with the fingertips, neither longer nor shorter. Certainly the weariness and boredom that claim to have exhausted life’s variety and pleasures are as old as Adam. But human capabilities have never been measured. So little has been attempted that precedent cannot tell us what anyone can do. Whatever your failures so far, “do not grieve, my child, for who can tell you what you have left undone?”

We could test our lives in a thousand simple ways. Consider, for example, that the sun ripening my beans shines at the same time on a whole system of worlds like ours. Remembering that would have spared me some mistakes. It was not in that light that I hoed my beans. What astonishing triangles have the stars as their points! How distant and different the beings in the universe’s many mansions who contemplate the same star at the same instant! Nature and human life vary as widely as our individual constitutions. Who can say what possibilities life holds for someone else? Could there be a greater miracle than seeing through one another’s eyes for a moment? In an hour we would inhabit every age of the world—yes, every world of every age. History, Poetry, Mythology! Nothing I have read of another’s experience would be as startling or instructive as that.

Much of what my neighbors call good I believe, in my soul, is bad. If I repent of anything, it will probably be my good behavior. What demon possessed me to behave so well? Say the wisest thing you can, old man—you who have lived seventy years with a certain kind of honor. I hear an irresistible voice calling me away from it all. Each generation abandons the previous generation’s projects like ships left stranded.

I believe we can safely trust far more than we do. For every measure of care we sincerely give elsewhere, we can give up as much care for ourselves. Nature accommodates our weakness as well as our strength. Some people’s constant strain and anxiety amount to an almost incurable illness. We are brought up to overestimate our work’s importance, yet how much happens without our doing it! What if we had fallen ill? How watchful we are, resolved never to live by faith if we can help it! All day we stay on guard; at night, reluctantly, we pray and hand ourselves over to uncertainty. We are so earnestly compelled to live in this way, revering our lives and denying that change is possible. This is the only way, we say. Yet there are as many ways as radii that can be drawn from a single center. Every change is a miracle to contemplate, and that miracle occurs every instant. Confucius said, “To know that we know what we know, and that we do not know what we do not know, that is true knowledge.” Once someone makes a fact imagined into a fact understood, I foresee everyone eventually building a life upon it.

Let us pause to consider what most of this trouble and anxiety concerns, and how much worry—or at least care—is really necessary. Living primitively, as on a frontier, even amid the outward signs of civilization, would have advantages. At least we would discover life’s basic necessities and the ways people have found to obtain them. We might even examine merchants’ old account books to see what people usually bought in shops—what they stored, in other words, the most basic groceries. Centuries of improvement have scarcely changed the essential laws of human existence, just as our skeletons probably cannot be distinguished from those of our ancestors.

By a _necessary of life_ I mean anything obtained through human effort that has always been, or through long use has become, so important that almost nobody tries to live without it, whether from savagery, poverty, or philosophy. In this sense many creatures need only one thing: Food. For a prairie bison that means a few inches of edible grass and drinking water, unless it seeks Shelter in a forest or mountain shade. No animal needs more than Food and Shelter. In this climate, human necessities can fairly be grouped as Food, Shelter, Clothing, and Fuel. Until we secure these, we cannot freely approach life’s real problems with any hope of success. Humanity has invented clothes and cooked food as well as houses. Perhaps the accidental discovery of fire’s warmth, followed by its use as a luxury, produced today’s necessity of sitting beside it. Cats and dogs acquire the same second nature before our eyes. Suitable Shelter and Clothing properly preserve our own internal heat. But too much of either, or of Fuel—external heat exceeding our internal heat—might reasonably be called the beginning of cooking us. The naturalist Darwin says that in Tierra del Fuego, while his warmly dressed party sat near a fire without being too warm, the naked savages farther away were, to his surprise, “streaming with perspiration at undergoing such a roasting.” Likewise, we are told, a New Hollander goes naked without harm while a European shivers inside his clothes. Can we not combine these savages’ hardiness with civilized people’s intellect? Liebig describes the body as a stove, with food as the fuel maintaining combustion inside the lungs. We eat more in cold weather, less in warmth. Animal heat comes from slow combustion; when it becomes too rapid, illness and death follow. Or the fire goes out through lack of fuel or a faulty draft. Vital heat must not, of course, be mistaken for fire; so much for the analogy. Our list suggests that _animal life_ and _animal heat_ are almost synonymous. Food is the Fuel maintaining our inward fire. Fuel itself merely prepares that Food or adds warmth from outside; Shelter and Clothing merely retain the _heat_ thus produced and absorbed.

Our bodies’ great need, then, is warmth: keeping their vital heat inside. What trouble we take over it, not only with Food, Clothing, and Shelter but with beds, our night-clothes! We rob birds’ nests and breasts to furnish this shelter within a shelter, like the mole’s bed of leaves and grass at the end of its tunnel. The poor man commonly calls this a cold world, and we blame much of our suffering directly on cold, physical as well as social. In some climates summer permits something like an Elysian life. Fuel is needed only to cook Food; the sun provides the fire and sufficiently cooks many fruits with its rays. Food is generally more varied and easier to find; Clothing and Shelter become partly or entirely unnecessary. In this country today, my experience puts a few tools—a knife, axe, spade, wheelbarrow, and so forth—next to necessities, together with lamplight, writing materials, and access to a few books for the studious. All cost very little. Yet some unwise people cross the globe to unhealthy, barbarous regions and devote ten or twenty years to trade so they may live—that is, stay comfortably warm—and finally die in New England. The luxuriously rich do not simply remain comfortably warm; they become unnaturally hot. As I suggested, they are cooked—naturally, _à la mode_.

Most luxuries and many so-called comforts are not merely unnecessary; they positively obstruct humanity’s advancement. In matters of comfort and luxury, the wisest have always lived more simply and sparingly than the poor. Nobody has been poorer in outward wealth or richer inwardly than the ancient Chinese, Hindoo, Persian, and Greek philosophers. We know little about them; the remarkable thing is that _we_ know as much as we do. The same holds for more recent reformers and benefactors of humanity. Only from the vantage point of what we would call voluntary poverty can anyone observe human life wisely and impartially. Luxury bears luxury as its fruit, whether in farming, trade, literature, or art. Today we have professors of philosophy, but no philosophers. Yet teaching it is admirable only because living it once was. A philosopher does more than think subtle thoughts or establish a school. He loves wisdom enough to obey it, living simply, independently, generously, and trustingly. He solves some of life’s problems in practice, not just in theory. Great scholars and thinkers usually succeed like courtiers, not kings or fully independent men. They manage to live by conforming, much as their fathers did, and never become ancestors of a nobler humanity. But why do people degenerate at all? Why do families decline? What kind of luxury weakens and destroys nations? Are we certain none of it enters our lives? Even in his outward arrangements, a philosopher lives ahead of his age. He eats, shelters, dresses, and warms himself differently from his contemporaries. How can anyone be a philosopher without maintaining his vital heat by better means than other people?

Once a person has warmed himself in these various ways, what comes next? Surely not more warmth of the same sort: more and richer food, larger and grander houses, more numerous and finer clothes, hotter fires burning more often and longer, and the like. After securing life’s necessities, he has another choice besides acquiring superfluities. He can now embark on life’s adventure, since his holiday from humbler labor has begun. The soil apparently suits the seed: its little root has struck downward, so it can confidently send its shoot upward too. Why has humanity rooted itself so firmly in the earth, except to rise as far into the heavens? We value nobler plants for the fruit they eventually bear in air and light, high above the ground. We do not treat them like lowly edible roots, which, even when biennial, are cultivated only until their roots mature, their tops often cut away for that purpose. Most people would not recognize them in flower.

I am not laying down rules for strong, courageous natures who will attend to their own affairs in heaven or hell. Perhaps they can build more magnificently and spend more freely than the richest without ever impoverishing themselves, hardly knowing how they live—if such people really exist, as some have dreamed. Nor do I address those who find their inspiration and encouragement in the world precisely as it is and cherish it with a lover’s enthusiasm and affection. To some degree I count myself among them. I am not speaking to people usefully occupied, whatever their circumstances; they know whether they are usefully occupied. I chiefly address the discontented multitude who idly complain about their hard lot or hard times when they could improve them. Some complain more forcefully and inconsolably than anyone precisely because, they say, they are doing their duty. I also have in mind that apparently wealthy class, the most terribly impoverished of all, who have piled up dross without knowing how to use it or discard it, and thereby forged their own gold or silver chains.

If I tried to describe how I have wanted to spend my life in past years, readers who know something of its actual history would probably be surprised. Those who know nothing of it would certainly be astonished. I will only suggest a few of the enterprises I have cherished.

Whatever the weather or the hour of night or day, I have wanted to seize the nick of time and notch it on my stick as well; to stand where the two eternities, past and future, meet—which is exactly the present moment—and toe that line. Forgive a little obscurity. My trade holds more secrets than most people’s, not because I choose to hide them, but because secrecy belongs to its nature. Gladly would I tell everything I know about it, never painting “No Admittance” on my gate.

Long ago I lost a hound, a bay horse, and a turtle-dove, and I still follow their trail. I have asked many travelers about them, describing their tracks and the calls they knew. One or two people I have met had heard the hound and the horse’s footsteps, and even watched the dove vanish behind a cloud. They seemed as eager to recover them as if the loss had been their own.

To be ahead not merely of sunrise and dawn, but, if possible, of Nature herself! How often, winter and summer, have I been out on my business before any neighbor stirred to attend to his! Many townsmen have surely met me coming back from this enterprise: farmers setting out for Boston in the twilight, or woodcutters heading to work. True, I never gave the sun any substantial help in rising. But merely being there, you may be sure, was of the utmost importance.

So many autumn days—and winter ones too—spent outside town trying to hear what was in the wind and carry its news by express! I almost sank my entire capital into this, and lost my breath as well, running against it. Had the matter concerned either political party, you can be sure the Gazette would have printed it among the earliest reports. At other times I watched from a cliff or tree, an observatory for telegraphing new arrivals. Or I waited on hilltops at evening for the sky to fall, hoping to catch something. I never caught much, and what I caught dissolved again in the sun, like manna.

For a long time I reported to a journal with a rather limited circulation, whose editor has still not thought fit to publish most of my contributions. Like so many writers, all I received for my trouble was my labor. In this case, however, the trouble rewarded itself.

For years I appointed myself inspector of snowstorms and rainstorms and faithfully performed the duty. If not a surveyor of highways, I surveyed woodland paths and shortcuts across fields. Wherever the public heel had proved their usefulness, I kept them open and the ravines bridged and passable throughout the year.

I have tended the town’s wild livestock, which trouble a conscientious herdsman considerably by jumping fences. I have watched over the farm’s unvisited corners and recesses, though I could not always tell whether Jonas or Solomon worked a particular field that day; it was no business of mine. I have watered red huckleberries, sand cherries, nettle trees, red pines, black ashes, white grapes, and yellow violets that might otherwise have withered in dry weather.

In short, I continued like this a long time, faithfully attending to my business—I can say that without boasting. Gradually it became clear that my townsmen would neither add me to the town’s officers nor make my position an easy office with a modest allowance. My accounts, which I swear I kept faithfully, have never actually been audited, much less approved, still less paid and settled. But I have not set my heart on that.

Not long ago a wandering Indian came to a well-known local lawyer’s house selling baskets. “Do you wish to buy any baskets?” he asked. “No, we do not want any,” came the answer. Leaving through the gate, the Indian exclaimed, “What! do you mean to starve us?” He had seen his industrious white neighbors prosper. The lawyer merely wove arguments and, as if by magic, acquired wealth and standing. So he had said to himself: I will enter business; I can weave baskets, and that is what I will do. He thought making them fulfilled his part, leaving it to the white man to buy. He had not discovered that he must make buying worthwhile to the other man, or persuade him it was worthwhile, or make something else worth buying. I too had woven a kind of finely textured basket, but had not made it worth anyone’s while to buy. That did not make weaving them any less worthwhile to me. Instead of studying how to persuade people to buy my baskets, I studied how to avoid having to sell them. The life people praise and call successful is only one kind of life. Why magnify one kind at the expense of every other?

Seeing that my fellow citizens were unlikely to give me a room in the courthouse, or a curacy or other paid living elsewhere, and that I must fend for myself, I turned more exclusively than ever toward the woods, where I was better known. I resolved to begin business immediately, without waiting to acquire the customary capital, using the slender resources already mine. I went to Walden Pond neither to live cheaply nor expensively, but to conduct some private business with as few obstacles as possible. Failing at that for lack of a little common sense, enterprise, or business ability would have seemed less sad than foolish.

I have always tried to develop exact business habits; everyone needs them. If you trade with the Celestial Empire, a little countinghouse on the coast, in some Salem harbor, supplies all the fixed establishment you need. Export what your country provides: entirely native products, plenty of ice and pine timber and a little granite, always in native-built ships. These will be sound ventures. You must personally oversee every detail, serving as pilot, captain, owner, and insurer all at once. Buy and sell and keep the accounts; read each incoming letter, and write or read every outgoing one; supervise unloading imports day and night; be almost simultaneously at many points along the coast—the richest cargo often comes ashore on a Jersey beach. Be your own telegraph, tirelessly scanning the horizon and hailing every passing coastal vessel. Keep goods moving steadily to supply that distant, exacting market. Stay informed about prices, prospects of war and peace everywhere, and approaching changes in trade and civilization. Profit from every exploring expedition’s discoveries, using new passages and every improvement in navigation. Study charts, establish the positions of reefs, new lights, and buoys, and continually correct the logarithmic tables. A calculator’s mistake often wrecks a ship on a rock when it should have reached a welcoming pier—consider the untold fate of La Perouse. Keep up with all science; study the lives of great explorers and navigators, adventurers and merchants, from Hanno and the Phœnicians to our own day. Finally, take stock from time to time so you know where you stand. Such work taxes all a man’s powers, with its problems of profit and loss, interest, tare and tret—the allowances for packing and waste—and measurements of every kind, demanding universal knowledge.

I have thought Walden Pond a promising place for business, and not just because of the railroad and ice trade. It offers advantages that prudence may forbid me to reveal: a good harbor and firm foundations. There are no Neva marshes to fill, although everywhere you must build on piles you have driven yourself. People say that a flood tide combined with a west wind and ice in the Neva would wipe St. Petersburg from the earth.

Since I proposed to start without the usual capital, it may be hard to imagine where I would obtain the means indispensable to any such undertaking. Let us turn straight to the practical question of Clothing. Perhaps novelty and other people’s opinions guide our purchases more often than real usefulness does. Anyone with work to do should remember that clothing’s first purpose is preserving vital heat, and its second, in our society, is covering nakedness. He can then judge how much necessary or important work he can accomplish without enlarging his wardrobe. Kings and queens who wear an outfit only once, though a royal tailor or dressmaker made it, cannot know the comfort of clothes that fit. They are no better than wooden racks for hanging clean laundry. Each day our clothes become more like us, taking on the wearer’s character, until discarding them requires almost the delays, medical aids, and solemnities attending the disposal of our bodies. A patch has never lowered anyone in my opinion. Yet people generally worry more about fashionable clothes—or at least clean, unpatched ones—than about a sound conscience. Even an unmended tear may reveal no worse vice than poor planning. Sometimes I test acquaintances by asking who could wear a patch, or merely two extra seams, over a knee. Most act as though it would ruin their prospects forever. They could more easily hobble into town with a broken leg than a torn trouser leg. A gentleman’s injured legs can often be repaired; his trousers, similarly injured, are beyond help. He considers not what deserves respect, but what receives it. We know few men, but a great many coats and breeches. Put your last shirt on a scarecrow and stand shirtless and shiftless beside it: who would not greet the scarecrow first? Passing a hat and coat on a stake in a cornfield the other day, I recognized the farmer. He was only a little more weather-beaten than at our last meeting. I have heard of a dog that barked at every clothed stranger approaching its master’s property but was readily soothed by a naked thief. How much social rank would survive if everyone’s clothes were removed? Could you reliably identify the most respected class in any gathering of civilized people? Traveling adventurously around the world from east to west, Madam Pfeiffer had reached Asiatic Russia, nearly home, when she felt obliged to change out of traveling clothes before meeting officials. She “was now in a civilized country, where —— — people are judged of by their clothes.” Even our democratic New England towns give almost universal respect to accidental wealth displayed only in clothing and carriages. The many people granting that respect remain, to that extent, heathens in need of a missionary. Besides, clothes brought sewing, work that may rightly be called endless: a woman’s dress, at least, is never finished.

A man who has finally found something to do need not buy a new suit for doing it. The old one gathering dust in the attic for an indefinite time will serve. Old shoes will serve a hero longer than his valet—if a hero ever keeps a valet. Bare feet are older than shoes, and he can manage with those. Only people attending soirées and legislative chambers need new coats, changing them as often as the person inside changes. If my jacket, trousers, hat, and shoes are fit for worshipping God, surely they will do? Who ever watched his old clothes, his actual old coat, wear completely out and return to their original elements, beyond being charitably passed to a poor boy, and perhaps by him to someone poorer still—or richer, shall we say, because he needs less? Beware, I say, of enterprises requiring new clothes instead of a new person to wear them. Without a new man, how can new clothes fit? Try any proposed enterprise in your old clothes. People need not something to _do with_, but something to _do_—or, better, something to _be_. Perhaps we should never buy a suit, however ragged or dirty the old one, until our conduct, enterprise, or voyaging makes us feel like new people inside it. Keeping it then would resemble putting new wine in old bottles. Like birds, we should molt only at a crisis in our lives. The loon retreats to lonely ponds for this. A snake sheds its skin, and a caterpillar its wormlike coat, through inner activity and growth. Clothes are only our outermost skin and mortal coil. Otherwise we sail under false colors and must finally be dismissed in disgrace by our own judgment as well as humanity’s.

We put on layer after layer as though, like exogenous plants, we grew by adding to the outside. Our outer clothes, often thin and fanciful, are an epidermis, a false skin with no share in our life, removable in places without fatal harm. Our heavier, constantly worn clothes form our cellular covering or cortex. Our shirts are our liber, our true bark: remove it and you girdle and destroy the man. I believe every people wears some equivalent of a shirt at certain seasons. A man should dress simply enough to find himself with his hands in the dark, and live so compactly and readily in every respect that, if enemies capture the town, he can follow the old philosopher out through the gate, empty-handed and untroubled. One thick garment generally serves as well as three thin ones, and cheap clothes really can be bought at prices customers can afford. A thick coat costs five dollars and lasts five years; sturdy trousers two dollars; cowhide boots a dollar and a half a pair; a summer hat a quarter-dollar; a winter cap sixty-two and a half cents—or a better one can be made at home for almost nothing. Who is so poor that, dressed like this in clothes _earned by himself_, he will find no wise people willing to honor him?

When I request a particular cut of clothing, my tailoress gravely replies, “They do not make them so now.” She puts no stress on “They,” as though citing an authority as impersonal as the Fates. Getting what I want is difficult simply because she cannot believe I mean it, that I dare be so rash. This oracular statement sends me into thought. I stress every word in turn, trying to uncover its meaning, discover the degree of kinship connecting _Them_ with _me_, and determine their authority over something so intimately mine. Finally I feel inclined to answer with equal mystery and no extra stress on “they”: “It is true, they did not make them so recently, but they do now.” What use is measuring me if she measures only my shoulders, like a peg to hang a coat on, rather than my character? We worship neither the Graces nor the Parcæ, but Fashion. She spins, weaves, and cuts with absolute authority. The chief monkey in Paris puts on a traveler’s cap, and every monkey in America copies him. Sometimes I despair of getting anything entirely simple and honest done with other people’s help. First we would have to put them through a powerful press to squeeze out their old notions, leaving them unable to regain their feet for some time. Even then someone would have a maggot in his head, hatched from an egg laid nobody knows when—for even fire cannot kill these things—and all the effort would be wasted. Still, let us remember that a mummy handed down some Egyptian wheat to us.

On balance, I do not think dressing has attained the dignity of an art here or anywhere else. People currently make do with whatever they can obtain. Like shipwrecked sailors, they put on what the beach offers, then laugh at one another’s disguises from a small distance in space or time. Each generation mocks old fashions while devoutly following new ones. Henry VIII.’s costume or Queen Elizabeth’s amuses us as much as the King and Queen of the Cannibal Islands’ would. Clothing separated from its wearer is always pathetic or grotesque. Only the serious eyes looking out and the sincere life within it restrain our laughter and make a people’s costume sacred. Give Harlequin a bout of colic, and his finery must suit that mood too. When a cannonball hits a soldier, rags become him as well as royal purple.

Men and women’s childish, savage appetite for fresh patterns keeps how many people shaking kaleidoscopes and peering through them to discover the figure this generation demands today! Manufacturers have learned how capricious the taste is. Two patterns differing only by a few threads of one color may have opposite fortunes: one sells immediately, the other stays on the shelf, though a season later the neglected one often becomes the height of fashion. By comparison, tattooing is hardly the hideous practice people call it. Printing is not barbarous merely because it goes skin-deep and cannot be altered.

I cannot believe our factory system is the best way for people to obtain clothes. Each day the workers’ condition more nearly resembles that of English workers. This is unsurprising: everything I hear and see suggests the chief purpose is unquestionably to enrich corporations, rather than clothe humanity well and honestly. In the long run people hit only the targets they choose. They had therefore better aim high, even if they miss at first.

As for Shelter, I acknowledge that it is now a necessity, although people have lived without it for long periods in colder countries than ours. Samuel Laing says that “the Laplander in his skin dress, and in a skin bag which he puts over his head and shoulders, will sleep night after night on the snow—in a degree of cold which would extinguish the life of one exposed to it in any woollen clothing.” He had watched them sleeping this way, yet adds, “They are not hardier than other people.” Probably humanity had not lived long on earth before discovering a house’s conveniences, the domestic comforts—a phrase that may originally have meant the comforts of a house more than those of a family. Those comforts must be limited and occasional in climates where houses suggest chiefly winter or the rainy season, and remain unnecessary for two-thirds of the year except as sunshades. Even in our climate, a summer shelter once served almost solely as a nighttime covering. In Indian gazettes a wigwam represented a day’s march; a row cut or painted on tree bark showed how many times the travelers had camped. Humanity was not so large-limbed and robust that it could avoid narrowing its world and walling off a space to fit itself. At first people were naked and outdoors. Pleasant enough on calm, warm days, that condition might have nipped the race in the bud during winters and rainy seasons, not to mention scorching sunshine, had people not hurried to clothe themselves in houses. According to the fable, Adam and Eve wore a bower before wearing other clothes. Humanity wanted a home, a place of warmth and comfort—first bodily warmth, then the warmth of affection.

We can imagine some enterprising mortal, in humanity’s infancy, crawling into a hollow rock for shelter. Every child starts the world afresh to some extent and loves being outside, even in cold and rain. Instinct leads it to play house as well as horse. Who does not remember the fascination of overhanging rocks and anything resembling a cave in childhood? That was the natural longing of the fragment of our earliest ancestor surviving in us. From caves we advanced to roofs of palm leaves, bark and branches, stretched woven linen, grass and straw, boards and shingles, stones and tiles. At last we no longer know open-air living, and our lives are domesticated in more ways than we realize. The hearth lies a long way from the field. Perhaps we would benefit from more days and nights with nothing between us and the heavenly bodies, from poets speaking less often beneath roofs and saints remaining there less constantly. Birds do not sing in caves, nor doves preserve their innocence in dovecots.

Anyone planning a home should exercise some Yankee shrewdness, lest he end up instead in a workhouse, a labyrinth without a guiding thread, a museum, almshouse, prison, or magnificent mausoleum. First consider how little shelter is absolutely necessary. Here in town I have seen Penobscot Indians living in thin cotton tents surrounded by nearly a foot of snow; I thought they might welcome deeper snow to keep out the wind. Formerly, the question of earning an honest living while retaining freedom for my proper pursuits troubled me more than it does now—unfortunately, I have grown somewhat callous. I used to notice a large box beside the railroad, six feet long and three wide, where workers locked their tools overnight. It occurred to me that anyone hard pressed could buy such a box for a dollar, bore a few auger holes for air, climb in at night or during rain, and hook down the lid, remaining free in love and free in soul. This seemed neither the worst alternative nor a contemptible one. You could sit up as late as you liked, then rise and go out without a landlord or house-lord pursuing you for rent. Many people are harried to death paying for a larger, more luxurious box who would not freeze to death in one like this. I am quite serious. Economy can be treated lightly, but cannot be disposed of that way. A hardy, primitive people, living mostly outdoors, once built comfortable houses here almost entirely from materials Nature placed ready to hand. Gookin, superintendent of the Indians under the Massachusetts Colony, wrote in 1674: “Their best houses are covered very neatly, tight and warm, with tree bark peeled from the trunks when the sap rises, and pressed while green into large sheets under heavy timber.... The poorer ones are covered with mats made from a kind of bulrush, and are reasonably tight and warm too, though less good than the former.... I have seen some sixty or a hundred feet long and thirty feet wide.... I have often slept in their wigwams and found them as warm as the best English houses.” He adds that skillfully embroidered mats generally carpeted and lined them, and various utensils furnished them. The Indians even controlled the wind’s effect with a mat hung above the roof opening and adjusted by a string. Such a dwelling took at most a day or two to build initially, and only a few hours to dismantle and reassemble. Every family owned one, or an apartment in one.

In the savage state, every family owns its own shelter, one as good as the best, and entirely sufficient for the coarser and simpler needs of the people living in it. Yet I believe I speak conservatively when I say that, although birds have nests, foxes holes, and savages wigwams, no more than half the families in modern civilized society own shelter. In large towns and cities, where civilization flourishes especially, owners form only a tiny fraction. Everyone else pays a yearly tax for this outermost garment, now indispensable in summer and winter. That payment could buy a village of Indian wigwams; instead it helps keep them poor all their lives. I am not chiefly arguing the disadvantages of renting rather than owning. Still, the savage clearly owns shelter because it costs little, while the civilized man usually rents because ownership is beyond his means—and ultimately renting is no more affordable. Someone objects that this payment buys the poor civilized man a dwelling palatial beside a savage’s. Twenty-five to a hundred dollars a year, the country rates, gives him centuries of improvements: spacious rooms, clean paint and wallpaper, a Rumford fireplace, plaster behind the walls, Venetian blinds, a copper pump, spring lock, roomy cellar, and much else. But why is the person supposedly enjoying these things generally a _poor_ civilized man, while the savage without them is rich as a savage? If civilization really improves the human condition—and I think it does, though only wise people use its advantages—it must provide better houses without making them costlier. A thing’s cost is the amount of what I call life exchanged for it, immediately or eventually. An average house nearby costs perhaps eight hundred dollars. Saving that amount consumes ten to fifteen years of a laborer’s life even without a family to support, valuing labor at a dollar a day, since some earn more and others less. Usually more than half his life will therefore pass before _his_ wigwam is earned. Renting instead offers only a doubtful choice between evils. Would a savage wisely exchange his wigwam for a palace on these terms?

You may guess that, for the individual, I reduce almost the entire advantage of holding surplus property as a reserve for the future to paying funeral expenses. Perhaps, though, a man is not actually required to undertake the business of burying himself. Still, this points to an important difference between civilized people and savages. Those planning for our benefit undoubtedly intend to make civilized life an _institution_, absorbing much of the individual’s life to preserve and perfect the race. But I want to show the sacrifice that currently purchases this advantage, and suggest that we might live so as to gain it all without suffering its disadvantages. What do you mean by saying the poor will always be with you, or that fathers ate sour grapes and their children’s teeth are set on edge?
“As surely as I live, says the Lord God, you will no longer have reason to use this proverb in Israel.”
“See, all souls belong to me; the father’s soul and the son’s soul alike are mine. The soul that sins is the one that shall die.”

Looking at my neighbors, Concord’s farmers, who are at least as prosperous as other classes, I find most have worked twenty, thirty, or forty years toward genuinely owning their farms. They usually inherited them burdened with debt or purchased them with borrowed money. We may count a third of that labor as their houses’ cost; generally they still have not paid for them. Sometimes the debt exceeds the farm’s value, making the whole farm one great burden; even then someone inherits it, saying he knows it well. When I ask the assessors, I am surprised they cannot immediately name twelve people in town owning their farms outright. For these homesteads’ histories, ask the banks holding their mortgages. A man who has actually paid for his whole farm through his own labor upon it is so rare in the neighborhood that all his neighbors know him and can point him out. I doubt Concord has three. The claim that the vast majority of merchants—even ninety-seven out of a hundred—must fail applies equally to farmers. One merchant points out, however, that many commercial failures are not genuine financial collapses but failures to keep inconvenient commitments: the collapse is moral. That makes matters infinitely worse. It also suggests that perhaps the other three fail to save their souls and are bankrupt in a worse sense than those who fail honestly. Bankruptcy and repudiated debts provide springboards for much of our civilization’s vaulting and somersaulting, while the savage stands on famine’s unyielding plank. Yet each year the Middlesex Cattle Show proceeds with _éclat_, as though every joint in agriculture’s machinery moved smoothly.

The farmer tries to solve the problem of making a living with a formula more complicated than the problem. To obtain shoelaces he speculates in cattle herds. With exquisite skill he sets a hair-trigger trap for comfort and independence; turning away, he catches his own leg in it. That explains his poverty, and something similar leaves us all poor in a thousand savage comforts despite our surrounding luxuries. As Chapman sings,—

“The false society of men—
—for worldly greatness
Turns every heavenly comfort into air.”

After acquiring his house, a farmer may find himself poorer rather than richer; the house may have acquired him. I think Momus had a sound objection to Minerva’s house: she “had not made it movable, by which means a bad neighborhood might be avoided.” The objection still holds. Our houses are such cumbersome property that they often imprison rather than house us, and the bad neighbors we ought to escape are our own shabby selves. I know at least one or two local families who have wanted for nearly a generation to sell houses on the outskirts and move into the village, but cannot manage it. Only death will release them.

Let us grant that the _majority_ eventually manage to own or rent modern houses with every improvement. Civilization has improved the houses more than the people meant to inhabit them. It has made palaces; creating actual noblemen and actual kings to live in them has proved considerably harder. And _if civilized people pursue nothing worthier than savages do, if most of their lives go merely to obtaining basic necessities and comforts, why should their dwellings be better?_

What becomes of the poor minority? Perhaps we will discover that as some rise in outward circumstances above the savage, others sink proportionately below him. One class’s luxury is balanced by another’s destitution: a palace on one side, the almshouse and “silent poor” on the other. The multitudes building pyramids as Pharaohs’ tombs lived on garlic and perhaps received no decent burial themselves. A mason finishing a palace cornice may return at night to a hut worse than a wigwam. The usual signs of civilization in a country do not prove that a vast part of its population lives any less degraded a life than savages. I mean the degraded poor here, not the degraded rich. To learn the truth of this for myself, I need look no farther than the shanties that line our railroads everywhere, those railroads that represent the latest improvement in civilization. On daily walks I see people living in pigsties, leaving the door open throughout winter for light, without a visible—or often imaginable—woodpile. Young and old alike have permanently contracted bodies from habitually shrinking against cold and misery; every limb and faculty is checked in its development. Surely we should examine the people whose labor accomplishes this generation’s distinguishing works. To varying degrees the same condition afflicts workers of every kind in England, the world’s great workhouse. Or consider Ireland, marked as a white, enlightened spot on the map. Compare the Irish people’s bodily condition with that of North American Indians, South Sea Islanders, or any savage race before contact with civilized people degraded it. I do not doubt that Ireland’s rulers are as wise as civilized rulers generally. Its condition merely proves how much squalor civilization can accommodate. I hardly need mention the laborers in our Southern States who produce our chief exports and are themselves one of the South’s chief products. But let me return to those said to live in _moderate_ circumstances.

Most people seem never to have considered what a house is. They remain needlessly poor all their lives because they suppose they must have one like their neighbors’. As though someone had to wear whatever coat a tailor chose to cut, or, gradually discarding a palm-leaf hat or woodchuck-skin cap, complained of hard times because he could not afford a crown! We could devise a house more convenient and luxurious still, which everyone would agree was beyond human means. Must we always try to acquire more, and never learn contentment with less? Should respectable citizens solemnly teach by example and instruction that a young man must, before dying, provide himself with a prescribed quantity of superfluous overshoes, umbrellas, and empty guest rooms for empty guests? Why cannot our furniture be as simple as an Arab’s or an Indian’s? When I picture humanity’s benefactors, exalted by us as heavenly messengers bringing divine gifts, I see neither a train of followers nor a wagonload of fashionable furniture. Suppose I conceded—what a curious concession!—that our furniture should exceed an Arab’s in complexity only as much as we exceed him morally and intellectually. At present it clutters and soils our houses. A good housewife would sweep most of it into the rubbish hole, refusing to leave her morning’s work unfinished. Morning work! By Aurora’s blushes and Memnon’s music, what ought our _morning work_ in this world to be? Three limestone pieces once sat on my desk. Discovering with horror that they needed daily dusting while my mind’s furniture remained undusted, I threw them out the window in disgust. How could I keep a furnished house, then? I would sooner sit outdoors: grass gathers no dust except where people have disturbed the soil.

The luxurious and self-indulgent set the fashions the herd follows so faithfully. Travelers lodging at the so-called best houses soon learn this. Innkeepers assume them to be Sardanapalus; surrender to that tender care, and they would soon be thoroughly emasculated. In railroad cars, I think we spend more on luxury than on safety or convenience. Without securing those, the carriage threatens to become merely a modern drawing room, full of divans, ottomans, sunshades, and a hundred other Oriental things carried westward—things invented for harem ladies and the effeminate inhabitants of the Celestial Empire, whose very names Jonathan ought to be ashamed to know. I would sooner have a pumpkin to sit on alone than share a crowded velvet cushion. Give me an earthly ride in an ox cart with freely circulating air rather than a journey to heaven in an excursion train’s fancy car, breathing _malaria_ the whole way.

The naked simplicity of primitive life had at least this advantage: people remained only temporary guests in Nature. Refreshed by food and sleep, a man considered his journey anew. His dwelling in the world was something like a tent as he threaded valleys, crossed plains, or climbed mountains. But look: people have become their tools’ tools. The person who independently picked fruit when hungry has become a farmer; the one sheltering under a tree, a housekeeper. We no longer camp as though for one night; we have settled on earth and forgotten heaven. We have adopted Christianity merely as a better method of _agri_-culture. For this world we built a family mansion, for the next a family tomb. The finest art expresses humanity’s struggle to escape this condition. Yet our art merely makes the low condition comfortable and the higher one forgettable. If a work of _fine_ art had come down to us, our village has nowhere suitable to place it. Our lives, houses, and streets supply no proper pedestal, no nail for a picture or shelf for a hero’s or saint’s bust. Considering how our houses are constructed, paid for—or not paid for—and internally managed and maintained, I wonder why the floor does not collapse beneath a visitor admiring the mantelpiece’s trinkets, dropping him into the cellar onto some honest, solid, if earthy foundation. I cannot miss the fact that this supposedly rich, refined life has been reached by a leap. I cannot enjoy its decorative _fine_ arts because the leap absorbs my attention. The greatest recorded leap achieved by human muscles alone, I remember, belongs to certain wandering Arabs said to have cleared twenty-five feet on level ground. Without artificial support, people beyond that distance necessarily return to earth. My first question to the proprietor of such great impropriety is: Who supports you? Are you among the ninety-seven failures or the three successes? Answer that, and perhaps I can admire your baubles as ornaments. The cart placed in front of the horse is neither a beautiful object to contemplate nor a useful arrangement for getting anywhere. Before decorating our houses with beautiful objects, we must strip their walls and strip our lives, laying foundations of beautiful housekeeping and living. And a taste for beauty develops best outdoors, where neither house nor housekeeper exists.

Old Johnson, describing this town’s first settlers, his contemporaries, in “Wonder-Working Providence,” says that “they burrow into the earth for their first shelter under a hillside, and, throwing soil over timber, make a smoky fire against the earth on the highest side.” They did not “provide themselves houses,” he says, “until the earth, through the Lord’s blessing, produced bread to feed them.” Their first harvest was so poor that “for a long time they had to cut their bread very thin.” Writing in Dutch in 1650 to inform prospective settlers, the secretary of the Province of New Netherland gives fuller details: “People in New Netherland, and especially New England, who cannot initially afford the farmhouses they want dig a square pit like a cellar, six or seven feet deep and as long and wide as they judge suitable. They case its earthen walls with wood and line the wood with tree bark or something similar to keep the earth from collapsing. They lay plank flooring, panel the ceiling overhead, raise a roof of poles, and cover those with bark or fresh turf. Thus their whole families can live dry and warm in these houses for two, three, or four years, with partitions dividing the cellars to suit the family’s size. At the colonies’ beginning, New England’s wealthy and leading men built their first homes this way for two reasons. First, they avoided wasting time on construction and going short of food the following season. Second, they did not discourage the many poor laborers they had brought from the Fatherland. After three or four years, when the country had been adapted to agriculture, they built handsome houses costing several thousands.”

Our ancestors’ method showed at least an appearance of prudence, as though they believed in satisfying the most urgent needs first. But have we satisfied those needs now? Thinking of acquiring a luxurious dwelling myself, I hesitate. The country, so to speak, is still unfit for _human_ cultivation, and we must slice our _spiritual_ bread far thinner than our forefathers sliced their wheat bread. I do not mean that even the simplest ages should neglect all architectural ornament. But let beauty first line our houses where they touch our lives, as it lines a shellfish’s home, rather than merely coat their surfaces. Alas, I have been inside one or two and know what actually lines them.

Although we are not so degenerate that we could no longer live in caves or wigwams or wear skins, accepting the advantages of human invention and industry is surely better, dearly bought though they are. Around here boards, shingles, lime, and bricks cost less and are easier to obtain than suitable caves, whole logs, sufficient bark, or even properly prepared clay and flat stones. I speak from knowledge, having studied the subject both theoretically and practically. A little more intelligence in using these materials could make us richer than today’s richest and turn civilization into a blessing. A civilized man is a wiser, more experienced savage. But let me hurry to my own experiment.

Toward the end of March 1845, I borrowed an axe and entered the woods beside Walden Pond near my intended house site. I began felling young white pines, tall and straight as arrows, for timber. Starting without borrowing is difficult; perhaps letting other people take an interest in your enterprise this way is the more generous course. Releasing the axe, its owner called it the apple of his eye. I returned it sharper than I received it. I worked on a pleasant pine-covered hillside, looking through the trees at the pond and at a small woodland clearing where pines and hickories were springing up. The pond’s ice had not melted, though open patches appeared; it was dark and soaked with water. Slight snow flurries came on some working days. For the most part, however, when I emerged from the trees onto the railroad as I made my way home after working there, the yellow sand embankment stretched gleaming through hazy air, the rails shone in spring sunlight, and larks, pewees, and other birds already returned to begin another year with us sang. Those pleasant spring days thawed humanity’s winter of discontent as well as the earth; dormant life began stretching. One day my axe head came loose. I cut a green hickory wedge, drove it in with a stone, and put the whole axe into a pool to swell the wood. A striped snake slid into the water and remained on the bottom, apparently comfortable, the entire time I stayed—more than a quarter-hour. Perhaps it had not fully emerged from its torpor. I thought a similar reason kept people in their present low, primitive condition. If the spring of springs awakened them, they would necessarily rise into a higher, more ethereal life. Previously, on frosty mornings, I had seen snakes on my path with parts of their bodies still numb and stiff, waiting for the sun to thaw them. On April 1 rain melted the ice. Early that very foggy day I heard a stray goose groping above the pond, cackling as though lost, or like the fog’s own spirit.
For several days I kept cutting and hewing the main timbers, studs, and rafters with my narrow axe. Few thoughts fit for sharing or for a scholar came to me; I sang to myself:—

I squared the main timbers to six inches, hewed most studs on just two sides, and the rafters and floor beams on one. Leaving the remaining bark intact made them as straight as sawn timber and much stronger. By now I had borrowed additional tools, so I carefully cut mortises or tenons into each piece beside its stump. My working days in the woods were not particularly long, but I generally brought bread and butter for dinner. At noon I sat among the fresh pine branches I had trimmed off and read the newspaper wrapped around it. My hands wore a thick layer of pitch, imparting something of the pines’ fragrance to my bread. By the time I finished, I was more a friend than an enemy to the pine tree, despite having felled some, because I knew it better. Now and then my axe drew a woodland wanderer, and we talked pleasantly over the chips I had made.

By mid-April my house frame was ready to raise: I did not hurry the work, but tried to make the most of it. For boards I had already bought the shanty of James Collins, an Irishman employed on the Fitchburg Railroad. His was considered an unusually fine shanty. He was away when I called to inspect it. I walked around outside, at first unseen from within because the window was set so high and deep. The little dwelling had a pointed cottage roof and little else visible, earth rising five feet around it like a compost heap. The roof was its soundest part, though sunlight had badly warped and embrittled it. There was no doorsill, just a permanent passage for hens beneath the door. Mrs. C. invited me inside; my approach drove the hens in too. It was dark, with mostly an earthen floor, damp, clammy, and feverish. A board here and there would not survive removal. She lit a lamp to display roof and walls and show that the wooden flooring continued under the bed. She warned me against stepping into the cellar, a sort of rubbish hole two feet deep. There were, she said, “good boards overhead, good boards all around, and a good window,” originally two unbroken panes, except that the cat had recently gone out that way. The entire contents were a stove, bed, sitting place, an infant in its birthplace, a silk parasol, a gilt-framed mirror, and a new patented coffee grinder nailed to an oak sapling. James returned while I was there, and we quickly struck a bargain. I would pay four dollars and twenty-five cents that evening; he would leave at five the following morning, selling to nobody else meanwhile; I would take possession at six. He advised arriving early to forestall some vague but entirely unjust claims for ground rent and fuel, the only encumbrance, he assured me. At six I passed the family on the road. Their whole property filled one large bundle—bed, coffee grinder, mirror, hens—except the cat. She fled to the woods and became wild, later, I learned, stepping into a woodchuck trap and finally becoming a dead cat.

That morning I dismantled the dwelling, pulled its nails, and carted it in small loads to the pond. There I spread the boards on the grass to bleach and straighten again in the sun. An early thrush offered a note or two as I drove the woodland path. A young Patrick betrayed his neighbor Seeley, another Irishman, by telling me that between loads Seeley pocketed the nails, staples, and spikes still straight and usable. On my return he would stand there greeting me, surveying the ruins with an unconcerned, fresh, springtime air; work was scarce, he said. He represented the spectators, helping to link this apparently insignificant event with the removal of Troy’s gods.

I dug my cellar into a south-facing hillside where a woodchuck had once burrowed. Through sumac and blackberry roots and below the last stain of vegetation, I excavated a space six feet square and seven deep, reaching fine sand where potatoes would never freeze in winter. I left the sides sloping and unlined with stone. Sunlight has never struck them, so the sand still stays in place. The work took only two hours. Breaking this ground gave me particular pleasure: in almost every latitude people dig into the earth for an even temperature. Under a city’s grandest house there is still a cellar for storing roots as of old; long after the upper structure disappears, descendants notice its hollow in the ground. A house remains only a kind of porch before a burrow’s entrance.

At last, early in May, several acquaintances helped me raise my frame, less because I needed help than because I welcomed the opportunity for neighborliness. Nobody ever had helpers whose character honored him more. I trust they will one day help raise higher structures. I moved in on July 4, once the boards and roof were on. Carefully tapered edges and overlapping boards made the house entirely rainproof. Before boarding it, I had laid a chimney foundation at one end, carrying two cartloads of stones uphill from the pond in my arms. I built the chimney in autumn after finishing my hoeing, before I needed fire for warmth. Meanwhile I cooked early each morning outdoors on the ground, a method I still find in some respects pleasanter and more convenient than the usual one. If a storm arrived before my bread finished baking, I set boards over the fire and sat beneath them watching the loaf, spending agreeable hours that way. With my hands so busy then, I read little. Yet the smallest paper scraps on the ground, my pot holder, or my tablecloth entertained me as much—indeed served the same purpose—as the Iliad.

Building even more deliberately than I did would be worthwhile. We might ask, for instance, what basis doors, windows, cellars, and attics have in human nature, perhaps raising nothing above the foundation until we find a better reason than even our immediate bodily needs. A person building his own house has something of the fitness of a bird constructing its nest. Who knows whether poetry would not develop in everyone if people built their homes by hand and provided food simply and honestly for themselves and their families, just as all birds sing while doing so? Alas, we imitate cowbirds and cuckoos, laying eggs in nests other birds have built and cheering no traveler with our unmusical chatter. Must we forever leave the carpenter the pleasure of building? What part does architecture play in most people’s actual experience? Throughout my walks I have never encountered anyone engaged in the simple, natural work of building his own house. We belong to the community. Not only the tailor is the ninth part of a man; so are the preacher, merchant, and farmer. Where will dividing labor end, and what purpose does it ultimately serve? Someone else certainly _may_ think for me. That does not make it desirable for him to prevent me from thinking for myself.

There are, admittedly, people called architects in this country. I have heard of at least one seized, as if by revelation, by the idea that architectural ornament should contain truth and necessity at its core, and therefore beauty. Perhaps that is good from his standpoint, but scarcely better than the usual dabbling. This sentimental architectural reformer began with the cornice instead of the foundation. He asked only how to put truth inside ornaments, so every sugarplum held an almond or caraway seed—though almonds are healthier without sugar, I maintain. He did not ask how the inhabitant could build truthfully within and without and leave ornament to itself. What sensible person ever supposed ornament was merely external and skin-deep, that a tortoise contracted for its spotted shell, or shellfish for mother-of-pearl colors, as Broadway’s inhabitants contracted for Trinity Church? A man should concern himself no more with his house’s architectural style than a tortoise with its shell’s. Nor should a soldier waste time painting the exact color of his courage on his flag. The enemy will discover it; when tested, he may turn pale. This architect seemed to lean over his cornice, timidly whispering a half-truth to rough occupants who understood it better. Every architectural beauty I see has grown gradually from within, from the needs and character of the inhabitant, the only real builder—from unconscious truthfulness and nobility, without concern for appearances. Any future beauty of this kind must likewise follow unconscious beauty in living. Painters know our most interesting dwellings are usually the poor’s unpretentious log huts and cottages. The inhabitants’ lives, for which these are shells, make them _picturesque_, not superficial peculiarities. A citizen’s suburban box will be equally interesting when his life is equally simple and pleasing to the imagination, and his house strives as little for effect. Much architectural decoration is literally hollow; a September gale could strip off these borrowed feathers without damaging anything substantial. Those with neither olives nor wine in their cellars can dispense with _architecture_. Suppose literary ornament received the same fuss, and the architects of our bibles spent as long on cornices as our church architects! Such methods produce the _belles-lettres_, the _beaux-arts_, and their professors. How terribly important, indeed, which way a few sticks slope above or below a man, or what colors coat his box! It would mean something if _he_ earnestly arranged and painted it. With the tenant’s spirit departed, however, he might as well build his coffin: architecture for the grave, with “carpenter” another word for “coffin-maker.” In despair or indifference, someone advises picking up earth at your feet and painting the house that color. Is he thinking of his final narrow house? A tossed coin could choose as well. What abundant leisure he must possess! Why pick up dirt? Better paint the house your own complexion; let it blush or pale for you. An enterprise to improve cottage architecture’s style! When my ornaments are ready, I shall wear them.

Before winter arrived I built the chimney and covered the already rainproof walls with shingles. They were imperfect, sappy pieces cut from the outside of logs, so I had to straighten their edges myself with a plane before putting them on.

Thus I have a snug, shingled, plastered house ten feet wide and fifteen long, with eight-foot posts, an attic and closet, a large window on either side, two trapdoors, an end door, and a brick fireplace opposite it. Paying the ordinary prices for my materials, but excluding all labor, which I supplied myself, I spent exactly the following amounts. I include the details because few people can state exactly what their houses cost, and fewer still, if any, know the separate prices of the materials making them up:—

Boards: $8.03½, chiefly boards from the shanty.
Discarded shingles for roof and sides: $4.00.
Laths: $1.25.
Two used windows, including glass: $2.43.
One thousand old bricks: $4.00.
Two casks of lime: $2.40. An expensive price.
Hair: $0.31. More than I required.
Mantel-support iron: $0.15.
Nails: $3.90.
Hinges and screws: $0.14.
Latch: $0.10.
Chalk: $0.01.
Transportation: $1.40. Much of it traveled on my back.
Total: $28.12½.

These include every material except timber, stones, and sand, which I claimed under a squatter’s rights. A small adjoining woodshed, built chiefly from material left over after constructing the house, belongs to my establishment too.
I intend to build a house outshining every house on Concord’s main street in grandeur and luxury, just as soon as it pleases me as much as my present one and costs no more.

I discovered that a student needing shelter can obtain it for a lifetime for no more than he currently pays in annual rent. If my boasting seems excessive, my excuse is that I boast for humanity, not merely myself; my own faults and inconsistencies do not alter my statement’s truth. Despite much cant and hypocrisy—chaff I struggle to separate from my wheat, and regret as much as anyone—I will breathe freely and stretch myself in this matter. It relieves both body and moral nature, and I refuse to become the devil’s advocate through humility. I shall try to speak well of truth. At Cambridge College, simply renting a room a little larger than mine costs thirty dollars yearly, though the corporation built thirty-two together beneath one roof. The student also endures numerous noisy neighbors and possibly a fourth-floor room. I cannot help thinking that if we possessed more genuine wisdom in these respects, we would need less education precisely because we would already have acquired a greater amount of it; and the financial expense of obtaining an education would to a very considerable degree disappear altogether. Conveniences at Cambridge or elsewhere cost the student or another person ten times as much life as proper management by both parties would require. The highest-priced things are never what the student needs most. Tuition, for example, occupies a large place in the term’s bill; the much more valuable education obtained among the most cultivated people of his generation costs nothing. Colleges are generally founded by collecting dollars and cents, then blindly carrying the division of labor to its extreme—a principle always requiring caution. A contractor is brought in to speculate on the undertaking; he hires Irishmen or other workers actually to lay the foundations, while prospective students supposedly prepare themselves for college. Successive generations pay for these oversights. I think it would be _better_ for students, or those hoping to benefit, even to lay the foundations themselves. A student who secures prized leisure and seclusion by systematically avoiding necessary human labor gets an ignoble, unprofitable leisure. He cheats himself of the experience that alone makes it fruitful. “But,” someone says, “you do not mean that students should work with their hands instead of their heads?” Not exactly, though he might think my meaning much the same. They ought not merely _play_ at life or _study_ it while the community pays for this costly game. They should seriously _live_ it from beginning to end. How could young people learn living better than by trying the experiment immediately? Surely it would exercise their minds as much as mathematics. To teach a boy arts and sciences, for example, I would not follow the usual practice of merely sending him near a professor, where everything except the art of living is taught and practiced. There he surveys the world through telescopes and microscopes, never his unaided eye; studies chemistry without learning how bread is made, mechanics without learning how it is earned; discovers Neptune’s new satellites without noticing specks in his own eyes or the vagabond around whom he himself revolves. He contemplates monsters in a drop of vinegar while surrounding monsters devour him. Who would advance further in a month: the boy making a pocketknife from ore he dug and smelted, reading what the task required, or the boy attending metallurgy lectures at the Institute and receiving a Rodgers’ penknife from his father? Which is likelier to cut his fingers?... Imagine my astonishment on leaving college when told I had studied navigation! A single trip down the harbor would have taught me more. Even the _poor_ student learns only _political_ economy; our colleges do not even sincerely profess that economy of living synonymous with philosophy. While reading Adam Smith, Ricardo, and Say, he consequently plunges his father hopelessly into debt.

Our colleges resemble a hundred other “modern improvements”: an illusion surrounds them, and real progress does not always occur. The devil continues collecting compound interest to the end on his initial share and repeated later investments. Our inventions are often attractive toys diverting us from serious matters. They improve the means without improving the end—an end already far too easy to reach, like Boston or New York by railroad. We hurry to build a magnetic telegraph between Maine and Texas, although perhaps neither has anything important to tell the other. Each may resemble the man eager for an introduction to a distinguished deaf woman who, once presented and handed one end of her ear trumpet, found he had nothing to say. As though rapid speech mattered more than sensible speech! We eagerly propose tunneling beneath the Atlantic, bringing the old world several weeks closer to the new; perhaps the first news leaking into America’s broad, flapping ear will be that Princess Adelaide has whooping cough. After all, a man whose horse trots a mile a minute carries no especially important message. He is no evangelist, traveling about on locusts and wild honey. I doubt Flying Childers ever took a peck of corn to the mill.

Someone tells me, “I wonder why you do not save money. You love traveling; today you could take the train to Fitchburg and see the country.” But I know better.
