It can be translated into every language, and not merely read but actually breathed from every human mouth—not just pictured on canvas or represented in marble, but carved from the very breath of life. The sign of an ancient man’s thought becomes the speech of a modern man. Two thousand summers have only given the monuments of Greek literature, like the Greeks’ marble statues, a richer golden, autumnal hue. They have brought their own calm, heavenly atmosphere into every land, protecting themselves against time’s corrosion. Books are the world’s treasured riches, the rightful inheritance of nations and generations. The oldest and finest books belong naturally and justly on the shelves of every cottage. They have no private cause to argue; as long as they illuminate and sustain their reader, his common sense will welcome them. In every society their authors form a natural aristocracy whose claim cannot be resisted, exercising more influence over humanity than kings or emperors. An unlettered and perhaps contemptuous trader wins the leisure and independence he has longed for through enterprise and hard work, and enters the circles of wealth and fashion. Inevitably he turns at last toward the still higher circles of intelligence and genius, which remain closed to him. He feels only how incomplete his education is, how vain and inadequate all his wealth. He gives further evidence of his good sense by taking pains to obtain for his children the intellectual cultivation whose absence he feels so sharply. In this way he becomes the founder of a family.

Anyone who has not learned to read the ancient classics in their original languages must know the history of humanity very imperfectly. Remarkably, no faithful copy of them has ever been made in a modern language—unless we count our civilization itself as such a copy. Homer has never yet appeared in English, nor Æschylus, nor even Virgil: works almost as delicate, as soundly made, and as beautiful as the morning itself. Whatever we say about the genius of later writers, they have seldom, if ever, matched the intricate beauty and finish of the ancients, or their lifelong, heroic labors in literature. The only people who talk of forgetting them are those who never knew them. There will be time enough to forget them once we possess the learning and genius needed to attend to them and appreciate them. What a rich age it will be when the relics we call Classics, and the nations’ still older, more than classical, yet even less familiar Scriptures, have accumulated further! Then the Vaticans will be full of Vedas and Zendavestas and Bibles, of Homers and Dantes and Shakespeares, and every coming century will have laid its trophies, in turn, in the world’s forum. With a pile like that we may hope to climb to heaven at last.

Humanity has never yet read the works of its great poets, because only great poets are capable of reading them. People have read them only as the crowd reads the stars: at best as astrologers, never as astronomers. Most people learn reading for some petty convenience, just as they learn arithmetic to keep their accounts and avoid being cheated in business. They know little or nothing of reading as a noble exercise of the mind. Yet this alone is reading in the highest sense: not a comfortable luxury that lulls us while our nobler powers fall asleep, but something we have to stretch up on tiptoe to read, something to which we must give our most alert and wakeful hours.

Once we have learned our letters, I think we ought to read the finest literature, instead of repeating our a b abs and our one-syllable words forever in the fourth or fifth classes, spending our whole lives on the lowest bench at the front. Most people are content to read, or hear someone read, one good book, the Bible, and perhaps to have its wisdom convict them. Then, for the rest of their lives, they vegetate and fritter away their abilities on what is called easy reading. Our Circulating Library has a work in several volumes called Little Reading; I thought the title must refer to some town of that name I had never visited. Some people can digest any quantity of this stuff, like cormorants or ostriches, even after the heartiest dinner of meat and vegetables: they let nothing go to waste. If some people are machines for supplying this fodder, others are machines for reading it. They read the nine-thousandth story of Zebulon and Sephronia, who loved as nobody had loved before, and whose true love did not run smoothly either—or, at any rate, how it ran, stumbled, picked itself up, and went on! Some poor unfortunate climbs a steeple, although he would have done better never to venture as high as the belfry. Having put him up there for no reason, the delighted novelist rings the bell to summon the whole world to hear—oh dear!—how he got down again! For my part, I would turn all these ambitious heroes of the universal kingdom of novels into human weathercocks, as heroes used to be placed among the constellations. Let them spin up there until they rust, without ever coming down to trouble honest people with their antics. The next time a novelist rings his bell, I shall not move, even if the meeting-house burns to the ground. “The Skip of the Tip-Toe-Hop, a Romance of the Middle Ages, by the celebrated author of ‘Tittle-Tol-Tan,’ to appear in monthly parts; a great rush; don’t all come together.” They read all this with eyes like saucers, with eager, primitive curiosity, and with a tireless gizzard whose ridges still need no sharpening. They read just as a four-year-old on his little bench reads his two-cent, gilt-covered Cinderella, with no improvement that I can detect in pronunciation, accent, or emphasis, and no greater skill in drawing out a moral or putting one in. The result is dimmed vision, stagnant vital circulation, and a general fainting and sloughing away of all the powers of the mind. Almost every oven bakes this gingerbread daily, more diligently than it bakes pure wheat bread or rye-and-Indian bread, and finds a more dependable market for it.

Even those called good readers leave the best books unread. What does our culture in Concord really amount to? Apart from a very few exceptions, this town has no taste for the finest books, or even for very good ones, in English literature, although everyone can read and spell their words. Here as elsewhere, even men who went to college and supposedly received a liberal education have little or no real familiarity with the English classics. As for humanity’s recorded wisdom—the ancient classics and Bibles, open to anyone willing to seek them out—scarcely any effort is made anywhere to get to know it. I know a middle-aged woodchopper who subscribes to a French newspaper. He says he does not want the news—he is above that—but wants to “keep himself in practice,” since he is Canadian by birth. When I ask what he thinks is the best thing he can do in this world, he says that, besides this, it is to maintain and improve his English. That is about all college-educated people generally do, or hope to do; for the same purpose they subscribe to an English newspaper. Suppose someone has just read one of the finest books in English: how many people will he find to discuss it with? Suppose instead that he has read a Greek or Latin classic in the original, a book whose reputation is familiar even to the supposedly illiterate. He will find nobody at all to talk to and must remain silent about it. Indeed, scarcely a professor in our colleges who has overcome the difficulties of the language has made equal progress with the wit and poetry of a Greek poet, or has any sympathetic understanding to offer an alert, heroic reader. And who in this town can even tell me the titles of humanity’s sacred Scriptures, its Bibles? Most people do not know that any nation besides the Hebrews has possessed a scripture. A man—any man—will walk a considerable distance out of his way to pick up a silver dollar. Yet here are golden words spoken by the wisest people of antiquity, their value vouched for by the wise of every later age. Still we learn to read only as far as Easy Reading, primers and schoolbooks; after school we settle for “Little Reading” and storybooks meant for boys and beginners. Our reading, conversation, and thought remain on a very low plane, fit only for pygmies and manikins.

I want to become acquainted with men wiser than those this soil of Concord has produced, men whose names are scarcely recognized here. Am I to hear Plato’s name and never read his book? That would be like having Plato as a fellow townsman and never seeing him, as my next-door neighbor and never hearing him speak or paying attention to the wisdom of his words. And what is the actual situation? His Dialogues, containing what was immortal in him, sit on the next shelf, and still I never read them. We are poorly bred, mean in our way of life, and illiterate. In this respect, I confess, I see no very great difference between the illiteracy of my neighbor who cannot read at all and that of the neighbor who has learned to read only books for children and feeble minds. We ought to be as good as the great people of antiquity, partly by first discovering how good they were. We are a race of titmouse-men; our intellectual flights scarcely rise above the columns of the daily newspaper.

Books are not all as dull as the people who read them. Somewhere there are probably words that speak exactly to our condition. If we could truly hear and understand them, they would do more for our lives than the morning or the spring, and might give the whole world a new appearance. How many people have dated a new period of their lives from the reading of a book! Perhaps the book exists that will explain our miracles to us and disclose new ones. Somewhere we may find expressed the things we cannot yet express. These very questions that trouble, puzzle, and bewilder us have come, in their turn, to every wise person; not a single question has been missed. Each has answered as well as he could, through his words and through his life. Along with wisdom, we will also learn generosity of mind. A solitary hired laborer on a farm outside Concord may have experienced a second birth and a particular religious awakening. He believes his faith drives him into silent solemnity and separation from others, and he may deny what I say. Yet thousands of years ago Zoroaster followed the same road and had the same experience. Being wise, he knew the experience was universal and treated his neighbors accordingly; he is even said to have invented and established worship among humankind. Let the laborer humbly enter into fellowship with Zoroaster, then, and, through the broadening influence of all the great and good, with Jesus Christ himself. Let “our church” go overboard.

We boast of belonging to the nineteenth century and of advancing faster than any other nation. But look how little this village does to cultivate its own mind. I have no wish to flatter my neighbors or to have them flatter me: neither of us would move forward that way. We need to be stirred up—prodded into a trot like the oxen we are. We have a reasonably good system of common schools, but they are schools for children only. For ourselves there is no school, apart from the half-starved winter Lyceum and, more recently, the feeble beginnings of a library proposed by the state. Almost any item for feeding or curing our bodies receives more money than the nourishment of our minds. It is time we had uncommon schools, time we stopped abandoning education just as we become men and women. It is time villages became universities and their older inhabitants became university fellows, with leisure—if they really are so prosperous—to pursue liberal studies for the rest of their lives. Must the world have only one Paris or one Oxford forever? Could students not board here and receive a liberal education under Concord’s skies? Could we not employ an Abelard to lecture to us? Alas, between feeding the cattle and minding the shop, we stay away from school too long, and our education is sadly neglected. In this country a village ought, in some ways, to fill the place occupied by a European nobleman. It should patronize the fine arts. It has money enough; only generosity of spirit and refinement are lacking. It readily spends money on things valued by farmers and traders. Propose spending on things that more intelligent people know to be far more valuable, and the proposal is called Utopian. Thanks to fortune or politics, this town has spent seventeen thousand dollars on a town-house. In a hundred years it will probably not spend as much on living intelligence, the real meat that belongs inside that shell. The hundred and twenty-five dollars subscribed each year for a winter Lyceum are better spent than any equal sum raised here. If ours is the nineteenth century, why not enjoy what the nineteenth century has to offer? Why should any part of our lives remain provincial? If we insist on newspapers, why not pass over Boston gossip and subscribe straight away to the best newspaper in the world? Why keep sucking the pap of “neutral family” papers or browsing on “Olive-Branches” here in New England? Send us the reports of every learned society, and we shall see whether they know anything. Why let Harper & Brothers and Redding & Co. choose our reading? A cultivated nobleman surrounds himself with everything that furthers his cultivation: genius, learning, wit, books, paintings, statues, music, philosophical instruments, and the like. Let the village do the same. Let it not stop at a schoolmaster, a parson, a sexton, a parish library, and three selectmen merely because our pilgrim forefathers once survived a cold winter on a bleak rock with those things. Acting together accords with the spirit of our institutions. Since our circumstances are more prosperous, I am sure our resources exceed the nobleman’s. New England can hire all the world’s wise people to teach her, taking turns to give them board and lodging, and need not be provincial at all. That is the _uncommon_ school we need. In place of noblemen, give us noble villages of men. If necessary, leave one bridge across the river unbuilt, and take a slightly longer way there. Throw at least one arch across the darker gulf of ignorance that surrounds us.

chapters.title: Sounds
paragraphs: But while we limit ourselves to books, even the finest classics, and read only particular written languages—which are themselves merely local dialects—we risk forgetting the language spoken without metaphor by all things and events, the only abundant and universal language. Much is published, little printed. Once the shutter is completely removed, we forget the rays that streamed through it. No system or training can replace the need for perpetual alertness. What is a course in history, philosophy, or poetry, however carefully chosen, or the finest company or most admirable daily routine, beside the discipline of always looking at what there is to see? Will you merely read and study, or will you see? Read your destiny, observe what lies before you, and walk forward into the future.

That first summer I read no books; I hoed beans. Often I did better still. Sometimes I could not afford to surrender the present moment’s bloom to work of either mind or hands. I love a wide margin around my life. On summer mornings, after my usual bath, I sometimes sat in my sunny doorway from sunrise until noon, absorbed in reverie among pines, hickories, and sumacs. In that undisturbed solitude and stillness, birds sang around me or passed soundlessly through the house. Only sunlight entering the west window or a traveler’s wagon rattling on the distant highway reminded me that time had passed. During those hours I grew like corn at night; they served me far better than manual labor would have. They were not time deducted from my life but an addition to my usual allowance. I understood what Orientals mean by contemplation and abandoning works. Generally I paid little attention to passing hours. The day advanced as though to illuminate some task of mine: morning became evening, and nothing memorable was accomplished. Instead of singing with the birds, I silently smiled at my endless good fortune. The sparrow on the hickory outside my door had its trill; I had a chuckle or stifled warble it might hear coming from my nest. My days were not weekdays stamped with heathen gods’ names, nor chopped into hours and fretted by a ticking clock. I lived like the Puri Indians, who, we are told, “for yesterday, to-day, and to-morrow they have only one word, and they express the variety of meaning by pointing backward for yesterday, forward for to-morrow, and overhead for the passing day.” Doubtless my townsmen called this sheer idleness. Judged by the standards of birds and flowers, however, I would not have failed. A man must, admittedly, find his occasions within himself. The natural day is calm and scarcely rebukes his laziness.

My way of life held at least one advantage over people who sought amusement elsewhere, in society or theaters: life itself had become my entertainment and never stopped being new. It was a drama with many scenes and no ending. If we truly kept getting our living and arranging our lives according to the latest, best method we had discovered, boredom would never trouble us. Follow your genius closely, and every hour it will reveal another prospect. Housework was agreeable recreation. When the floor grew dirty I rose early, put all my furniture on the grass, bed and bedstead in one bundle, and splashed water and white pond sand onto the floor. I scrubbed with a broom until it shone clean and white. By the time villagers finished breakfast, morning sunshine had dried the house enough to move back in, scarcely interrupting my reflections. Seeing my entire household piled on the grass like a gypsy’s pack delighted me. My three-legged table stood among pines and hickories, still bearing books, pen, and ink. The things themselves seemed glad to escape and reluctant to return. Sometimes I wanted to stretch an awning over them and sit outside. Sunlight and free wind playing over them were worth seeing and hearing: familiar objects look so much more interesting outdoors. A bird perches on the next branch, life-everlasting grows beneath the table, blackberry vines wind around its legs, and pinecones, chestnut burrs, and strawberry leaves scatter nearby. It seemed those shapes must originally have found their way onto tables, chairs, and bedsteads because the furniture once stood among them.

My house stood on a hillside at the edge of the larger wood, surrounded by young pitch pines and hickories. A narrow footpath ran downhill the half-dozen rods to the pond. In front grew strawberries, blackberries, life-everlasting, johnswort, goldenrod, scrub oaks, sand-cherry, blueberry, and groundnut. Late in May, sand-cherry (_Cerasus pumila_) decorated the path with delicate flowers clustered in umbels cylindrically around short stems. By autumn those stems, heavy with handsome, good-sized cherries, bent into garlands radiating in every direction. I tasted these cherries out of a wish to pay Nature a compliment, though I could scarcely call their flavor palatable. Sumac (_Rhus glabra_) flourished around the house, pushing through my embankment and growing five or six feet its first season. Its broad, feathered, tropical-looking leaves were strange but pleasing. Large buds suddenly emerged late in spring from dry, apparently dead sticks and magically unfolded into graceful, tender green branches an inch thick. Sometimes, sitting at my window, I heard a fresh branch fall to the earth like a fan without the slightest breeze. Its heedless growth had strained its weak joints until its own weight broke it. In August the large berry clusters, which had attracted many wild bees as flowers, gradually became bright, velvety crimson. Again their weight bent and broke the tender limbs.

As I sit by the window this summer afternoon, hawks circle the clearing. Wild pigeons give the air a voice with their headlong rush, crossing my view in twos and threes or perching restlessly in the white pine behind the house. A fishhawk dimples the pond’s glassy surface and rises with a fish; a mink slips from the marsh outside my door and seizes a frog along the shore. Reed-birds flit about, bending the sedges beneath them. For half an hour railroad cars have rattled in my hearing, their sound fading and reviving like a partridge’s drumming, carrying Boston travelers into the country. I was not as remote from the world as a boy I heard about, sent to work for a farmer in the eastern part of town. He soon ran home, worn down and homesick. Never had he seen so dull and isolated a place; everybody had gone away—why, you could not even hear the whistle! I doubt Massachusetts has such a place now:—

“Truly our village now has become the target
Of one of those swift railroad arrows; over
Our peaceful plain its soothing sound is—Concord.”

The Fitchburg Railroad reaches the pond about a hundred rods south of my home. I usually walk its embankment into the village, linked to society, as it were, along this line. Freight-train workers traveling the whole route pass me so often that they bow as to an old acquaintance. Apparently they take me for an employee; and so I am. I too would gladly repair a track somewhere along the earth’s orbit.

Winter and summer the locomotive’s whistle pierces my woods like a hawk shrieking over a farmyard. It announces restless city merchants entering the town’s circle, or adventurous country traders arriving from the opposite direction. Appearing beneath one horizon, they shout across to the other to clear the track; sometimes two towns hear the warning. Here are your groceries, countryside; here are your rations, countrymen! No farmer is independent enough to refuse them. And here is payment! screams the countryman’s whistle: timber, like long battering rams, drives twenty miles an hour toward the city walls, with enough chairs to seat all its weary and burdened inhabitants. In this huge, cumbersome act of politeness, the country offers the city a chair. Every Indian huckleberry hill is stripped; every cranberry meadow raked into the city. Cotton comes up, woven cloth goes down; silk comes up, woolens go down; books come up, while the intelligence that writes them goes down.

When I meet an engine and its cars moving off like a planet—or rather a comet, since nobody seeing its speed and direction knows whether it will ever return to this system, its orbit showing no returning curve—I watch the steam banner streaming behind in gold and silver wreaths. It resembles the soft clouds I have seen high overhead, spreading their masses toward the light, as though this traveling demigod, this cloud-compeller, might soon dress his retinue in sunset’s colors. When the iron horse snorts thunder that echoes in the hills, shakes the earth beneath its feet, and breathes fire and smoke through its nostrils—I wonder what winged horse or fiery dragon the new Mythology will make of it—the earth seems at last to have inhabitants worthy of it. If only everything were as it looked, and people enlisted the elements for noble purposes! If that steam cloud were the sweat of heroic deeds, or as beneficent as a cloud over a farmer’s fields, Nature herself and the elements would gladly accompany people on their errands as escorts.

I watch morning trains pass with the same feeling as sunrise, which is hardly more regular. Their cloud-train trails far behind and rises higher and higher, heading for heaven while the cars head for Boston. It hides the sun briefly and shades my distant field. Beside this celestial train, the little earthbound cars are merely the spear’s barb. This winter morning the iron horse’s keeper rose early among the mountains by starlight to feed and harness his steed. Fire also awoke early to supply its vital heat and start it moving. If only the enterprise were as innocent as it is early! In deep snow they put on its snowshoes and use a giant plow to cut a furrow from mountains to sea. The following cars, like a seed drill, scatter the country’s restless people and circulating merchandise as seed. All day the fire-steed flies across the land, pausing only for its master to rest. At midnight its footfalls and defiant snort wake me as it confronts the elements in a remote wooded glen, sheathed in snow and ice. Only the morning star brings it to its stall, before another departure without rest or sleep. Or at evening I hear it in its stable venting the day’s surplus energy, calming nerves and cooling liver and brain for a few hours of iron slumber. If only the undertaking were as heroic and commanding as it is lengthy and tireless!

Deep in unfrequented woods along town boundaries, where once only hunters ventured by day, these brilliant parlors now dart through the darkest nights without their occupants knowing. One moment they stop at a brightly lit town or city station among a sociable crowd; the next they enter the Dismal Swamp, startling fox and owl. Departures and arrivals now mark the village day’s epochs. Their punctual precision and far-reaching whistle let farmers set clocks by them: one well-run institution regulates a whole countryside. Has the railroad not improved punctuality? Do people not speak and think faster at stations than they once did at stagecoach offices? There is something distinctly electrifying about the very atmosphere of this new place compared with the old stagecoach office. Its miracles astonish me: neighbors I would have confidently predicted could never catch such a prompt conveyance to Boston are ready when the bell sounds. Doing things “railroad fashion” is now proverbial. There is value in a power warning us so frequently and earnestly to leave its track. Here nobody pauses to read the riot act or shoot over the crowd’s heads. We have built a fate, an _Atropos_, that never swerves. Give your engine that name. People receive notice that at an exact hour and minute these bolts will fly toward specified compass points. Yet business continues undisturbed; children walk to school on the other track. The arrangement steadies our lives. We are all trained as sons of Tell. Invisible bolts fill the air. Every path but your own belongs to fate; keep to your own track, then.

What attracts me to commerce is its courage and enterprise. It does not fold its hands and pray to Jupiter. Daily I see these men doing business with some measure of contentment and bravery, achieving more than they realize, perhaps working better than they could deliberately have planned. The heroism of men who spent half an hour in Buena Vista’s front line moves me less than the steady, cheerful courage of those making a snowplow their winter quarters. They possess not only the three-in-the-morning courage Bonaparte thought rarest; their courage stays awake longer. They sleep only when the storm sleeps or their iron steed’s sinews freeze. Perhaps this morning of the Great Snow, still raging and chilling everyone’s blood, I hear their engine bell muffled within the bank of fog formed by their chilled breath. It announces the cars _are coming_, without much delay, despite a New England northeast blizzard’s veto. I see snow- and frost-covered plowmen, their heads above the blade that turns under something other than daisies and field mice’s nests, like Sierra Nevada boulders occupying an outermost place in the universe.

Commerce has an unexpected confidence and serenity: alert, adventurous, tireless. Its methods are also natural, much more so than many fanciful enterprises and sentimental experiments, which explains its remarkable success. I feel refreshed and enlarged when freight cars rattle by, smelling the goods that distribute their odors all the way from Long Wharf to Lake Champlain. They recall foreign lands, coral reefs, Indian oceans, tropical climates, and the globe’s vast extent. Palm leaves destined to cover so many fair-haired New England heads next summer, Manilla hemp, coconut husks, old rope, gunny sacks, scrap iron, and rusty nails make me feel more a world citizen. This carload of torn sails is more readable and interesting now than as paper made into printed books. Who could describe their storms as vividly as the tears in them do? These proof sheets need no corrections. Here comes Maine timber spared by the last flood, its price up four dollars a thousand because other timber washed to sea or splintered. Pine, spruce, cedar—first, second, third, fourth grades—so recently all one grade, waving above bear, moose, and caribou. Next, a prime lot of Thomaston lime will travel far among the hills before being slaked. Baled rags of every color and quality represent cotton and linen at their lowest stage, dress’s final result. Their patterns are no longer promoted—unless in Milwaukie—as splendid English, French, or American prints, ginghams, muslins, and so forth. Collected from fashion and poverty everywhere, they will become paper of one color or a few shades, on which someone will write supposedly factual tales of real life, high and low! This closed car smells of salt fish, New England’s strong commercial scent, recalling the Grand Banks and fisheries. Who has not seen salt fish so thoroughly cured for this world that nothing can spoil it, shaming the saints’ perseverance? You could sweep or pave streets with it, split kindling, or shelter driver and load against sun, rain, and wind behind it. A trader could hang it beside his door as a sign on opening his business, as one Concord trader did, until his oldest customer could not decide whether it was animal, vegetable, or mineral. Yet it would remain pure as a snowflake and, boiled in a pot, emerge as excellent dun fish for Saturday dinner. Next come Spanish hides whose tails keep the same twist and upward angle they had when their oxen galloped across the Spanish main’s pampas. They exemplify obstinacy, showing how nearly hopeless and incurable inborn faults are. Practically speaking, once I know someone’s real disposition I expect no change for better or worse in this life. As the Orientals say, “A cur’s tail may be warmed, and pressed, and bound round with ligatures, and after a twelve years’ labor bestowed upon it, still it will retain its natural form.” The only cure for stubbornness like these tails’ is making glue of them, their usual fate, I believe; then they stay put and stick. Here is a hogshead of molasses or brandy addressed to John Smith, Cuttingsville, Vermont, some Green Mountains trader importing for farmers near his clearing. Perhaps he stands now above his cellar door considering the latest coastal arrivals and their effect on his prices. He tells customers, for the twentieth time this morning, that prime-quality supplies should arrive on the next train. The Cuttingsville Times advertises them.

While these goods travel up, others travel down. A whizzing sound draws me from my book, and I see a tall pine felled on far northern hills. Having flown across the Green Mountains and the Connecticut, it shoots like an arrow through the township in ten minutes, almost unseen by other eyes, going

“to serve as the mast
Of some great admiral’s ship.”

Listen! The cattle train arrives carrying the cattle of a thousand hills: sheepfolds, stables, and cow yards airborne, drovers with sticks and shepherd boys among their flocks. Everything except the mountain pastures whirls past like leaves blown from mountains in September gales. Calves and sheep bleat, oxen jostle, and the air sounds as though a whole pastoral valley were passing. The old bellwether rattles its bell at the front; mountains truly skip like rams and little hills like lambs. Amid them rides a carload of drovers, now level with their herds, their occupation gone but their useless sticks still gripped as badges of office. Where are the dogs? To them it is a stampede. They are completely baffled and have lost the trail. I seem to hear them barking behind the Peterboro’ Hills or panting up the Green Mountains’ western slope. They will miss the kill. Their occupation too has disappeared; loyalty and shrewdness trade below par. They will creep back to their kennels disgraced, or perhaps run wild and ally with fox and wolf. Thus your pastoral life is whisked past and away. But the bell rings; I must clear the track and let the cars pass:—

What does the railroad mean to me?
I never go to see
Where it ends.
It fills some hollows,
Builds banks for swallows,
Sets the sand blowing,
And blackberries growing,
but I cross it as I would a woodland cart track. I refuse to let its smoke, steam, and hissing blind my eyes or ruin my ears.

Now the trains and all the restless world have passed, and the pond’s fish no longer feel their rumble, I find myself more completely alone than ever. Perhaps throughout the long afternoon only a faint carriage or wagon rattle on the distant highway interrupts my thoughts.

On some Sundays, when the wind favored it, I heard Lincoln’s, Acton’s, Bedford’s, or Concord’s bells: a faint, sweet, almost natural melody worth importing into the wilderness. After traveling far enough over the woods, the sound acquires a particular vibrating hum, as if it swept the pine needles on the horizon like the strings of a harp. Every sound heard at the greatest possible distance produces this same effect, a vibration of the universal lyre. In much the same way, the intervening atmosphere lends a distant ridge of earth an azure color that makes it interesting to our eyes. The melody reaching me had been strained through the air and conversed with every woodland leaf and needle. It was the portion of sound the elements had absorbed, modulated, and echoed from valley to valley. An echo is partly an original sound, and there lies its magic and charm. It does more than repeat what deserves repeating in the bell: partly it is the woods’ own voice, the same ordinary words and notes sung by a wood-nymph.

At evening a cow lowing beyond the woods on the far horizon sounded sweet and musical. At first I mistook it for singers who sometimes serenaded me, perhaps roaming hill and valley. Soon the sound lengthened into the cow’s inexpensive, natural music, disappointing me not unpleasantly. I am not trying to satirize the young men at all, but rather to express my appreciation of their singing, when I say I clearly heard its kinship with the cow’s music. Ultimately both formed a single expression of Nature.

For part of summer, whippoorwills regularly chanted evening prayers for half an hour at seven-thirty, after the evening train. They perched on a stump outside my door or on the roof’s ridgepole. Almost as precise as clockwork, they began within five minutes of a fixed time relative to sunset each evening. I had an unusual chance to study their habits. Sometimes four or five called simultaneously from different parts of the wood, one accidentally a measure behind another. They came close enough for me to distinguish not only the cluck following each note but often a peculiar buzzing like a fly trapped in a spiderweb, only proportionately louder. Sometimes a bird circled repeatedly within a few feet of me in the woods, as though tied by a string; probably I stood near its eggs. They sang intermittently all night, becoming as musical as ever just before and around dawn.

When other birds fall silent, screech owls resume the song, chanting their ancient u-lu-lu like mourning women. Their miserable cry truly belongs in Ben Jonson. Wise midnight witches! It is not the poets’ straightforward, honest tu-whit tu-who. In all seriousness, it is a solemn graveyard song, suicide lovers consoling one another in infernal groves with memories of heavenly love’s pain and joy. Yet I love their wailing and sorrowful answers trilling along the woods. Sometimes they recall music and songbirds, as though expressing music’s dark, tearful side, regrets and sighs yearning for song. They are spirits, depressed spirits and melancholy forebodings, of fallen souls that once roamed earth at night in human form, doing dark deeds. Now they expiate their sins with wailing hymns and laments in the landscapes of their offenses. They reveal afresh the variety and capacity of Nature, our shared dwelling. _Oh-o-o-o-o, I wish I had never been bor-r-r-r-n!_ sighs one beside the pond, restlessly circling to another perch in the gray oaks. Then _I wish I had never been bor-r-r-r-n!_ answers another across the water with trembling sincerity, and _bor-r-r-r-n!_ comes faintly from distant Lincoln woods.

A hooting owl also serenaded me. Close by, its voice might seem Nature’s saddest sound, as though she wished permanently to fix a dying person’s moans in her choir: some weak remnant of mortality, past hope, howling like an animal yet sobbing humanly as it enters the dark valley. A gurgling musical quality makes it more terrible—I begin with gl when imitating it—as though its mind had reached a gelatinous, moldy stage in the decay of all healthy, courageous thought. It recalled ghouls, idiots, and insane howling. But then an answer came from far woods, made genuinely musical by distance: _Hoo hoo hoo, hoorer hoo_. In fact, heard winter or summer, night or day, it generally brought only pleasant associations.

I am glad owls exist. Let them supply humanity’s idiotic, mad hooting. Their sound perfectly suits swamps and twilight woods that daylight never explains, suggesting an immense, undeveloped Nature people have failed to recognize. They embody the stark twilight and unfulfilled thoughts within everyone. All day sunshine has rested on a wild swamp where a solitary spruce wears usnea lichens, small hawks circle overhead, chickadees lisp among evergreens, and partridge and rabbit hide below. Now a grimmer, more fitting day begins, and another race of creatures wakes to express what Nature means there.

Late at night I heard distant wagons rumbling across bridges, a sound traveling farther than almost anything else after dark. Dogs bayed, and sometimes a forlorn cow lowed again in a faraway barnyard. Meanwhile bullfrogs trumpeted along the entire shore: stout spirits of ancient drinkers and revelers, unrepentant still, attempting a round in their Stygian lake—may Walden’s nymphs forgive the comparison, for there are frogs here although hardly any weeds. They try to maintain their former banquets’ merry customs, though their voices are now hoarse and solemnly deep, mocking merriment. Wine has lost its flavor, becoming mere liquid to swell their bellies. Sweet drunkenness no longer drowns the past; only saturation, waterlogging, and bloating remain. Beneath the northern shore the most aldermanlike frog rests his chin on a heart-leaf, a napkin for his slobbering jaws. He takes a deep swallow of once-despised water and passes the cup, crying _tr-r-r-oonk, tr-r-r-oonk, tr-r-r-oonk!_ Immediately the password crosses from a distant cove, where the next in seniority and girth has drunk to his appointed mark. After the ritual circles the shore, the master of ceremonies says _tr-r-r-oonk!_ with satisfaction. Each repeats it in turn, down to the least swollen, leakiest, flabbiest belly, leaving no doubt. Again and again the bowl circles, until sunshine disperses the morning mist. Only the patriarch remains above water, vainly bellowing _troonk_ occasionally and pausing for an answer.

I cannot be sure I ever heard a cock crow from my clearing. I thought keeping a cockerel simply for its music, like a songbird, might be worthwhile. This once-wild Indian pheasant surely has the most remarkable birdcall. If it could become established without being domesticated, its voice would soon be our woods’ most famous, surpassing goose clangor and owl hoots. Imagine hens filling the pauses with cackling while their lords’ trumpets rested! No wonder humanity added this bird to its domestic stock, quite apart from eggs and drumsticks. Picture a winter morning’s walk in woods full of them, their native woodland, with wild cocks crowing from trees, clear and piercing for miles across the echoing earth, drowning other birds’ weaker calls! Whole nations would wake to attention. Who would not rise early, earlier each day throughout life, until becoming indescribably healthy, wealthy, and wise? Poets everywhere celebrate this foreign bird alongside their native singers. Brave Chanticleer suits every climate, more indigenous even than the natives. Always healthy, sound of lung, he never loses spirit. Sailors wake to his voice on Atlantic and Pacific alike; its shrillness never interrupted my sleep. I kept no dog, cat, cow, pig, or hens, so you might have thought domestic sounds lacking. No churn or spinning wheel, not even a singing kettle, hissing urn, or crying children provided comfort. An old-fashioned man would have gone mad or died of boredom by then. Not even rats lived in the walls: they had starved, or rather never been lured in. Only squirrels on the roof and beneath the floor; a whippoorwill on the ridgepole; a blue jay screaming under the window; a hare or woodchuck under the house; a screech-owl or cat-owl behind it; wild geese or a laughing loon on the pond; and a fox barking at night. Even larks and orioles, those gentle birds of cultivated ground, never visited the clearing. No crowing cockerels or cackling hens in a yard. No yard! Only unfenced Nature up to the windowsills. Young woods rise beneath your meadows; wild sumacs and blackberry vines break into the cellar. Sturdy pitch pines, short of room, rub and creak against the shingles, their roots reaching underneath the whole house. Instead of a gale taking a hatch or shutter, it snaps or uproots a pine behind your house for fuel. Instead of the Great Snow leaving no path to your front-yard gate, there is no gate, no front yard, and no path to the civilized world!

chapters.title: Solitude
paragraphs: What a delicious evening this is: the whole body becomes a single sense, drinking pleasure through every pore. I move back and forth in Nature with a strange freedom, as a part of her. Walking the pond’s rocky shore in my shirtsleeves, though the air is cool, cloudy, and windy, I find every element unusually friendly, even without anything particular to catch my attention. The bullfrogs sound their trumpets to announce the night, and the whippoorwill’s call comes across the water on the rippling wind. My fellow feeling with the fluttering leaves of the alders and poplars almost takes my breath away. Yet my calm, like the lake’s, has ripples without being disturbed. These little waves stirred by the evening breeze are as far from a storm as the smooth, reflecting surface is. Darkness has fallen, but the wind still blows and roars through the woods, the waves still break, and some creatures sing the others to sleep. The resting is never complete. The wildest animals are not resting; now they seek their prey. Fox, skunk, and rabbit wander fearlessly through woods and fields. They are Nature’s watchmen, joining one day of living activity to the next.

On coming home, I find signs that visitors have called and left their cards: a handful of flowers, perhaps, a wreath of evergreen, or a name penciled onto a yellow walnut leaf or a wood chip. People who seldom enter the woods pick up some little fragment of the forest to play with as they walk, then leave it behind, on purpose or by accident. Someone has stripped a willow twig, bent it into a ring, and left it on my table. I could always discover whether anyone had visited while I was away, from bent grass or twigs or the marks of shoes. Usually I could also judge their sex, age, or kind from some small trace—a dropped flower, a tuft of grass pulled up and tossed aside—even as far away as the railroad, half a mile off. A lingering smell of pipe or cigar told me too. Indeed, the smell of a traveler’s pipe often informed me that he was passing along the highway sixty rods away.

Usually we have enough room around us. Our horizon never comes quite up to our elbows. Neither the dense woods nor the pond lies immediately at our door. There is always a little clearing, familiar and worn by our use, claimed and somehow fenced off, reclaimed from Nature. Why have people left this vast tract and circuit to me, these several square miles of seldom-visited forest, for my private enjoyment? My nearest neighbor lives a mile away. Within half a mile of my house, no other house can be seen except from the hilltops. I have the entire forest-bounded horizon to myself, with a distant glimpse of the railroad where it meets the pond on one side, and of the fence alongside the woodland road on the other. For the most part my home is as solitary as the prairies. It is as much Asia or Africa as New England. I have, so to speak, a sun and moon and stars of my own, a whole little world to myself. No traveler ever passed my house at night or knocked on my door, any more than if I had been the first man or the last. The exceptions came in spring, when, at long intervals, people from the village arrived to fish for pouts. Plainly they did most of their fishing in the Walden Pond within themselves, baiting their hooks with darkness. Soon they withdrew, generally with nearly empty baskets, leaving “the world to darkness and to me.” No human neighborhood ever intruded on the night’s black core. I believe people are still somewhat afraid of the dark, despite all the witches having been hanged and Christianity and candles having been introduced.

Yet I have sometimes found the sweetest, gentlest, most innocent and heartening companionship in any object in Nature, even for a miserable hater of humanity or the most melancholy man. No very dark melancholy can overtake someone who lives amid Nature and still possesses his senses. No storm has ever been anything but Æolian music to a healthy, innocent ear. Nothing has a rightful power to force a simple, courageous man into commonplace sadness. As long as I have the seasons for friends, I trust nothing can make my life a burden. The soft rain watering my beans and keeping me indoors today is not dreary or depressing; it benefits me as well. It keeps me from hoeing, but it is worth far more than my hoeing. Even if it lasted long enough to rot the seeds underground and ruin the potatoes in the low-lying fields, it would help the grass on the uplands; and whatever helps the grass helps me. At times, comparing my life with other men’s, I seem to enjoy greater favor from the gods than they do, far beyond any merit I know of in myself. It is as though the gods have given me a pledge and guarantee that my fellows lack, and offer me particular guidance and protection. I am not flattering myself; if such a thing is possible, they are flattering me. Only once have I ever felt lonely, or in the least weighed down by solitude. A few weeks after I moved into the woods, I spent an hour wondering whether close human neighbors were necessary to a calm and healthy life. Being alone felt unpleasant. Even then, however, I recognized a slight madness in my mood and seemed to anticipate getting over it. While I was thinking these thoughts in a gentle rain, I suddenly felt such sweet and kindly companionship in Nature—in the very patter of the drops and in every sight and sound around my house—that the supposed advantages of human neighbors dwindled to nothing. All at once an infinite, inexplicable friendliness supported me like the atmosphere itself. I have never thought about those advantages since. Each little pine needle opened and swelled with sympathy, offering me its friendship. I became so vividly aware of something akin to me, even in surroundings we habitually call wild and dreary, and aware that my closest relation, the most human presence, was neither a person nor a villager, that I thought no place could ever feel strange to me again.—

Some of my happiest hours came in the long spring and autumn rainstorms that kept me at home all afternoon as well as all morning. Their unending roar and pelting soothed me; an early dusk brought on a long evening, giving many thoughts time to take root and open out. When driving northeast rains put the village houses to such a test, with maids waiting in the front halls, mop and bucket ready to keep out the flood, I sat behind my own door. My little house was all front hall, and I thoroughly enjoyed its shelter. During one heavy thunderstorm, lightning struck a large pitch-pine on the far side of the pond. It cut a striking, perfectly regular spiral groove from top to bottom, at least an inch deep and four or five inches across, as one might carve a walking stick. The other day I passed it again. Looking up at that scar, now clearer than ever, I felt awe at the terrible, irresistible bolt that had descended from the harmless sky eight years earlier. People often tell me, “I should think you would feel lonesome down there, and want to be nearer to folks, rainy and snowy days and nights especially.” I am tempted to answer: this whole inhabited earth is only a speck in space. How far apart do you imagine the two most distant inhabitants of that star live, when our instruments cannot even measure the width of its disk? Why should I be lonely? Does our planet not belong to the Milky Way? Your question does not strike me as the most important one. What kind of space separates a person from his fellows and makes him solitary? I have discovered that no amount of walking brings two minds much closer together. What do we most want to live near? Surely not a crowd of people, the station, post office, barroom, meeting-house, schoolhouse, grocery, Beacon Hill, or the Five Points, where people gather most thickly. We want to be near the everlasting source of our life, from which our experience has always shown it flowing, just as a willow stands beside the water and stretches its roots toward it. This place differs with different natures, but it is where a wise man will dig his cellar.... One evening on the Walden road I caught up with a townsman who had amassed what people call “a handsome property”—although I never had a _fair_ view of it. He was driving two cattle to market and asked how I could persuade myself to give up so many comforts of life. I told him I was quite sure I liked it tolerably well; I meant it seriously. Then I went home to bed, leaving him to find his way through darkness and mud to Brighton—or Bright-town—where he would arrive sometime in the morning.

For a dead man, any prospect of waking or returning to life makes the choice of time and place immaterial. Wherever that may happen is always the same place, indescribably pleasing to every sense. Usually we let passing, peripheral circumstances supply the occasions of our lives. In fact, those circumstances are what distract us. The power that shapes a thing’s existence is what lies nearest to it. _Right beside_ us, the greatest laws are constantly being carried out. The workman _right beside_ us is not the one we hired and so enjoy talking to, but the workman whose handiwork we ourselves are.
“How immense and deep is the influence of the subtle powers of Heaven and Earth!”
“We try to see them but cannot see them; we try to hear them but cannot hear them. They are one with the substance of things and cannot be separated from it.”

“They move people throughout the universe to cleanse and sanctify their hearts, and to put on their festive clothing to offer sacrifices and gifts to their ancestors. It is an ocean of subtle intelligences. They are everywhere: above us, to our left, to our right; on every side they surround us.”

We are the subjects of an experiment that I find more than a little interesting. Under these circumstances, can we not spare ourselves the company of our fellow gossips for a while and find cheer in our own thoughts? Confucius speaks truly when he says, “Virtue does not remain as an abandoned orphan; it must of necessity have neighbors.”

Thought allows us to be beside ourselves in a perfectly sane way. By a deliberate effort of mind we can stand apart from deeds and their results, letting everything, good or bad, rush past us like a torrent. We are not entirely caught up in Nature. I can be the driftwood carried by the stream, or Indra in the sky looking down upon it. A performance in a theater _may_ move me; an actual event that seems to concern me far more closely _may not_. I know myself only as a human being, a scene, so to speak, where thoughts and feelings occur. I sense a certain doubleness that lets me stand as far from myself as from someone else. No matter how intense an experience is, I am aware of the presence and judgment of a part of me that is, as it were, no part of me at all. It is a spectator, participating in none of the experience but observing it; and it is no more me than it is you. Once life’s play—perhaps its tragedy—ends, the spectator goes on his way. For him it was a kind of fiction, simply a work of imagination. This doubleness can readily make us poor friends and neighbors at times.

I find spending most of my time alone good for my health. Company, even the finest company, soon grows tiring and scatters my attention. I love being by myself. No companion I have ever found offers such companionship as solitude. Usually we are lonelier when we go out among other people than when we remain in our rooms. Wherever he happens to be, someone thinking or working is always alone. You cannot measure solitude by the miles separating a man from his fellows. A truly hardworking student in one of Cambridge College’s crowded hives is as solitary as a dervish in the desert. A farmer can spend a whole day alone in woods or fields, chopping or hoeing, without feeling lonely, because he is occupied. Yet when he gets home at night, he cannot sit by himself in a room at the mercy of his thoughts. He must go somewhere he can “see the folks,” enjoy himself, and, as he thinks, repay himself for his solitary day. Consequently he wonders how a student can sit alone indoors all night and most of the day without boredom and “the blues.” What he fails to understand is that, though indoors, the student is still working in _his_ field and chopping in _his_ woods, just as the farmer does in his own. In turn the student seeks the same recreation and companionship as the farmer, though perhaps in a more concentrated form.

Companionship is generally sold too cheaply. We see one another so often that we have no time to acquire any fresh value for each other. Three times a day we meet over meals and give one another another taste of the stale, musty cheese we are. We have had to settle on rules called etiquette and politeness to make these constant encounters bearable and keep them from turning into open warfare. We meet at the post office, at social gatherings, and around the fire every evening. We crowd together, get in one another’s way, and trip over each other; I think this costs us some of our mutual respect. Certainly we could meet less often and still communicate everything important and heartfelt. Think of the factory girls, never alone, scarcely even in their dreams. Things would be better if there were only one person to each square mile, as where I live. A man’s value is not in his skin, that we should have to touch him.

I have heard about a man who was lost in the woods and lay dying of hunger and exhaustion at the foot of a tree. His loneliness was eased by grotesque visions that his disordered imagination, weakened with his body, placed around him and that he took to be real. In the same way, bodily and mental health and strength may give us the constant comfort of a similar but more normal and natural companionship, until we understand that we are never alone.

My house is full of company, especially in the morning, when nobody visits. Let me offer several comparisons; perhaps one will give some idea of my circumstances. I am no lonelier than the loon laughing so loudly on the pond, or than Walden Pond itself. What company does that solitary lake enjoy, pray tell? Yet its waters, with their azure color, hold blue angels rather than blue devils. The sun is alone, except in thick weather, when it sometimes seems there are two suns; but one of them is a mock sun. God is alone—but the devil is very far from alone. He entertains plenty of company; he is legion. I am no lonelier than a lone mullein or dandelion growing in a pasture, a bean leaf, sorrel, a horsefly, or a bumblebee. I am no lonelier than Mill Brook, a weathercock, the north star, the south wind, an April rain shower, a January thaw, or the first spider to inhabit a new house.

On long winter evenings, with snow falling thickly and wind howling in the woods, I am sometimes visited by an old settler, the original owner. He is said to have dug Walden Pond, lined it with stones, and edged it with pine woods. He tells me tales of ancient time and new eternity, and between us we spend a cheerful evening in friendly merriment and pleasant reflections, even without apples or cider. He is a wonderfully wise and humorous friend, whom I love dearly. He conceals himself more thoroughly than Goffe or Whalley ever did; and though people suppose him dead, nobody can point out his grave. An elderly woman also lives in my neighborhood, unseen by most people. Sometimes I love to walk in her fragrant herb garden, gathering medicinal plants and listening to her fables. Her imagination is incomparably fertile, and her memory reaches back beyond mythology. She can tell me the origin of every fable and the facts on which it rests, because the events happened when she was young. A rosy, vigorous old woman, she takes pleasure in every season and every kind of weather, and may yet outlive all her children.

Nature’s innocence and kindness are beyond description—the innocence and kindness of sunshine, wind, and rain, of summer and winter. What health and cheer they keep giving us! Their sympathy with humankind is so constant that, if anyone ever grieved for a truly just cause, all Nature would feel it: the sun would lose its brightness, the winds would sigh with human feeling, the clouds would weep rain, and the woods would shed their leaves and dress in mourning in the middle of summer. Should I not be in communication with the earth? Am I not myself partly leaves and vegetable mold?

What pill will keep us healthy, tranquil, and content? Not a remedy from my great-grandfather or yours, but the universal vegetable and botanical medicines of our great-grandmother Nature. With these she has always kept herself young, outlived so many old Parrs, and nourished her health on their decaying abundance. For my cure-all, spare me the quack bottles of a mixture dipped from Acheron and the Dead Sea, brought out of those long, low wagons resembling black schooners that we sometimes see fitted up to carry bottles. Give me a drink of pure morning air instead. Morning air! If people refuse to drink it at the day’s fountainhead, then we must bottle some and sell it in shops for those who have lost their season ticket to the world’s mornings. But remember: even in the coolest cellar it will hardly keep until noon. Long before then it will force out the stoppers and follow Aurora’s footsteps westward. I do not worship Hygeia, daughter of the old herb doctor Æsculapius, whom monuments show with a serpent in one hand and a cup in the other, from which the serpent sometimes drinks. I worship rather Hebe, Jupiter’s cupbearer, the daughter of Juno and wild lettuce, who could restore gods and people to the vigor of youth. She was probably the only completely sound, healthy, robust young lady ever to walk this earth, and wherever she arrived, spring arrived with her.

chapters.title: Visitors
paragraphs: I believe I enjoy company as much as most people, and am quite ready to attach myself temporarily, like a leech, to any full-blooded person crossing my path. I am no natural hermit. If business took me to a barroom, I might outstay even its most persistent regular.

My house held three chairs: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society. When unexpected numbers arrived, the third chair had to serve them all, though they generally saved space by standing. How many great men and women fit inside a little house is surprising. Twenty-five or thirty souls, bodies included, have gathered under my roof at once; often we parted without feeling we had come particularly close. Many public and private houses strike me as extravagantly oversized for their occupants, with countless rooms, huge halls, and cellars storing wine and other munitions of peace. Their size and magnificence reduce the people inside to vermin infesting them. When a herald sounds his summons before a Tremont, Astor, or Middlesex House, I marvel to see the entire population emerge as a ridiculous little mouse creeping across the veranda, soon slipping back into a crack in the pavement.

One drawback of my little house was the difficulty of getting far enough from a guest when we began expressing large thoughts in large words. You need to leave space for your thoughts to arrange their sails for the voyage and run a course or two before finally making their port. The bullet of your thought must settle from sideways movement and ricochets into its final steady course before entering a listener’s ear, or it may plow out through the side of his head. Our sentences also needed an interval in which to unfold and arrange their columns. Like nations, individuals need broad, natural boundaries, even substantial neutral territory between them. Talking across the pond to someone opposite has seemed a special luxury. Indoors we were too close even to begin hearing; we could not speak quietly enough to be heard. It was like dropping two stones so near together in calm water that their ripples destroy each other. Mere loud chatter lets us stand cheek by jowl, feeling one another’s breath. Thoughtful, restrained speech requires distance, allowing bodily heat and moisture to evaporate. To commune most intimately with whatever in each of us lies beyond or above direct address, we need silence and usually enough physical separation that hearing one another’s voices would be impossible anyway. Measured by this standard, speech exists for the hard of hearing. Many delicate things cannot be said by shouting. As our conversation grew loftier and grander, we pushed our chairs farther apart until they touched opposite corners; even then the room generally proved too small.

My “best” room, my withdrawing room, always prepared for visitors and with a carpet sunlight seldom reached, was the pine wood behind the house. On summer days I took distinguished guests there. An invaluable household servant swept its floor, dusted its furniture, and kept everything in order.

A lone guest sometimes shared my simple meal. Stirring a hasty-pudding or watching a loaf rise and finish baking in the ashes did not interrupt our talk. But if twenty people sat in the house, nobody mentioned dinner, even if there was bread for two; it was as though eating had gone out of practice. We naturally abstained, treating that not as a breach of hospitality but as the most considerate and suitable course. Bodily wear and decay, so frequently needing repair, seemed miraculously slowed; vital energy held firm. I could entertain a thousand this way as readily as twenty. If anyone ever left hungry or disappointed when I was home, he may be sure I at least shared his feelings. Establishing better new customs instead of old ones is that easy, though housekeepers doubt it. There is no need for you to make your whole reputation as a host rest on the dinners you provide. No Cerberus ever deterred me from visiting as effectively as one man’s elaborate fuss over feeding me. I took it as a circuitous, exquisitely polite request never to trouble him again that way. I doubt I shall return. For my cabin’s motto I would proudly adopt the lines of Spenser a visitor wrote on a yellow walnut leaf as his card:—

“Arriving there, they fill the little house,
And seek no entertainment where none is;
Rest is their feast, and everything suits their will:
The noblest mind finds the greatest contentment.”

Winslow, later governor of Plymouth Colony, once walked through the woods with a companion on a formal visit to Massasoit. Tired and hungry on reaching his lodge, they received a royal welcome but heard no mention of food all day. At night, in their words, “He placed us on the bed with himself and his wife, them at one end and us at the other: merely planks a foot above the ground with a thin mat. Two more of his principal men, short of room, crowded beside and upon us, leaving us more exhausted by our lodging than our journey.” At one the following afternoon, Massasoit “brought two fish he had shot,” each about three times the size of a bream. “After they were boiled, at least forty people expected shares. Most ate some. This was our sole meal in two nights and a day; had one of us not bought a partridge, we would have begun our journey fasting.” They feared growing dizzy from hunger and sleeplessness, caused by “the savages’ barbarous singing (for they sang themselves to sleep),” and departed while they still had strength to reach home. Their lodging certainly provided poor comfort, though the inconvenience was undoubtedly intended as an honor. Concerning food, however, I cannot see how the Indians could have done better. They themselves had nothing to eat and wisely recognized that apologies could not feed guests. So they tightened their belts and left the matter unspoken. Another visit by Winslow, during a plentiful season, lacked nothing in that respect.

People, at any rate, are unlikely to be lacking anywhere. During my woodland life I had more visitors than at any other period—meaning I actually had some. I met several people there under circumstances far more favorable to our meeting than I could have found for them anywhere else. Fewer came on trivial errands: distance alone sifted my company. I had retreated far into solitude’s great ocean, into which society’s rivers empty, so that, for my needs, mostly only the finest sediment settled around me. Evidence also drifted over of unexplored, uncultivated continents on the far shore.

Who arrived this morning but a genuine Homeric or Paphlagonian man! His name is so fitting and poetic that I regret being unable to print it. A Canadian woodcutter and post-maker, he can bore holes in fifty posts daily, and ate a woodchuck caught by his dog for his last supper. He too has heard of Homer. Without books, he says, he “wouldn’t know what to do on rainy days,” though perhaps many rainy seasons have passed since he read one completely. Far away in his native parish, a priest able to pronounce Greek taught him to read his verse in the testament. Now, while he holds the book, I must translate Achilles’ rebuke to Patroclus for looking so sorrowful: “Why are you in tears, Patroclus, like a young girl?”—

“Or have you alone received some news from Phthia?
They say Menœtius, Actor’s son, is still alive,
And Peleus, son of Æacus, lives among the Myrmidons;
If either had died, we would grieve deeply.”

“That’s good,” he says. Under his arm is a large bundle of white-oak bark gathered this Sunday morning for a sick man. “I suppose there’s no harm in going after such a thing to-day,” he remarks. Homer to him was a great writer, though he had no idea what Homer wrote about. A simpler, more natural person would be hard to find. Vice and disease, spreading such gloomy moral colors across the world, scarcely seemed to exist for him. About twenty-eight, he had left Canada and his father’s home twelve years earlier to work in the States, saving toward a farm, perhaps eventually back in his own country. Nature cast him in the roughest mold: a stout, sluggish body gracefully carried, thick sunburned neck, bushy dark hair, and dull, sleepy blue eyes occasionally bright with expression. He wore a flat gray cloth cap, a dingy wool-colored overcoat, and cowhide boots. He ate a great deal of meat, usually carrying dinner in a tin pail to work a couple of miles beyond my house; he chopped throughout summer. Cold meat, often woodchuck, accompanied coffee in a stone bottle dangling from his belt by a string. Sometimes he offered me a drink. He passed early across my bean-field, without a Yankee’s anxious rush toward work. He had no intention of hurting himself and did not mind earning only his board. Often, if his dog caught a woodchuck along the way, he would leave dinner in the bushes and walk a mile and a half back to clean the animal and store it in his boardinghouse cellar. First he would spend half an hour considering whether he could safely sink it in the pond until evening; he loved lingering over such questions. Passing in the morning, he would say, “How thick the pigeons are! If working every day weren’t my trade, hunting would give me all the meat I wanted—pigeons, woodchucks, rabbits, partridges—by gosh! One day would get me enough for a week.”

He was an accomplished woodcutter, adding flourishes and ornament to his craft. He cut trees level and near the ground so new shoots would grow vigorously and sledges could pass over the stumps. Rather than leave an entire tree standing to support his stacked firewood, he trimmed it to a narrow stake or splinter, finally small enough to break off by hand.

He fascinated me by being so quiet, solitary, and happy, a well of good humor and contentment overflowing through his eyes. There was nothing mixed or adulterated in the mirth that came from him. Sometimes I found him felling trees; he greeted me with an indescribably satisfied laugh and Canadian French, though he also spoke English. As I approached he stopped working, stretched along a fallen pine, and, half suppressing laughter, peeled off inner bark, rolled it into a ball, and chewed while talking and laughing. His animal spirits were so exuberant that a thought tickling him sometimes sent him tumbling and rolling on the ground with laughter. Looking at the trees, he would exclaim, “By George! Chopping here amuses me well enough; I want no better sport.” Sometimes he spent a whole free day strolling in the woods with a pocket pistol, firing himself salutes at regular intervals. In winter he warmed his coffee in a kettle over a noonday fire. Sitting on a log at dinner, he sometimes had chickadees land on his arm and peck the potato in his fingers. He said he “liked having the little _fellers_ around.”

The animal side of humanity was chiefly developed in him. In bodily endurance and contentment he was kin to rock and pine. Once I asked whether a full day’s labor ever left him tired at night. With complete seriousness and sincerity he answered, “Gorrappit, I never was tired in my life.” His intellectual and so-called spiritual sides, however, slept as in a baby. His education followed the innocent, ineffective method Catholic priests use with aborigines: teaching trust and reverence without awakening consciousness, keeping a child a child rather than making him a man. Nature gave him a strong body and contentment, then supported him on every side with reliance and reverence, letting him live his seventy years as a child. He was so genuine and unsophisticated that an introduction would explain him no better than introducing a woodchuck to a neighbor. The neighbor must discover him as you had. He would play no part. People paid him for labor and thus helped feed and dress him, but he exchanged no opinions with them. His humility was so natural and simple—if someone with no aspirations can be called humble—that it was no separate quality he could conceive. Wiser people were demigods. Hearing one would visit, he acted as though such grandeur could expect nothing from him, but would assume every responsibility and allow him to remain forgotten. Praise never reached his ears. Writers and preachers especially commanded his reverence; their performances were miracles. When I said I wrote a good deal, he long supposed I meant handwriting, since his own was remarkably fine. Sometimes beside the road I found his native parish’s name beautifully traced in snow, its French accent correct, and knew he had passed. Did he ever want to write his thoughts? He had read and written letters for people unable to do so, he replied, but never attempted thoughts. No, he could not: where would he begin? It would kill him, with spelling to manage at the same time!

I heard that a distinguished thinker and reformer asked whether he wanted the world changed. Apparently unaware anyone had ever considered the question, he chuckled in surprise and replied in his Canadian accent, “No, I like it well enough.” Dealing with this man would have suggested many things to any philosopher willing to do so. A stranger would think him ignorant of things generally. Yet sometimes I glimpsed someone I had never seen before, unable to decide whether he was wise as Shakespeare or ignorant as a child, subtly conscious like a poet or merely stupid. A townsman told me that seeing him stroll through the village in his little close-fitting cap, whistling, suggested a prince in disguise.

His only books were an almanac and an arithmetic; he was quite proficient in the latter. The almanac served as an encyclopedia, supposedly summarizing human knowledge, as indeed it largely does. I enjoyed asking his views on current reforms. He had never heard of them but unfailingly considered them in the simplest, most practical way. Could he manage without factories? He had worn homemade Vermont gray, he answered, and found it good. Could he dispense with coffee and tea? Did the country provide any drink besides water? He had soaked hemlock leaves in water and drunk the result, which he preferred to plain water in hot weather. Asked whether he could live without money, he explained its convenience in terms matching the most philosophical explanations of its origin, even the derivation of _pecunia_. Suppose he owned an ox and needed needles and thread from a shop: continually mortgaging a corresponding piece of the creature would be inconvenient and soon impossible. He defended many institutions better than philosophers because describing their direct effects on him revealed why they really prevailed; speculation had supplied no alternative reason. Once, on hearing Plato defined a man as a featherless biped, and someone displayed a plucked cock as Plato’s man, he thought the _knees_ bending the wrong way an important difference. Sometimes he exclaimed, “How I love to talk! By George, I could talk all day!” After months without seeing him, I once asked if summer had brought him a new idea. “Good Lord,” he said, “someone working like me does well just not to forget the ideas he already has. Maybe the man hoeing beside you wants to race; then, by gorry, your mind has to be there, thinking about weeds.” Sometimes he asked first whether I had made an improvement. One winter day, hoping to suggest an inward substitute for the external priest and a higher reason for living, I asked whether he was always satisfied with himself. “Satisfied!” he said. “Some men are satisfied with one thing, others with another. A man with enough might be content to sit all day with his back to the fire and his belly to the table, by George!” No maneuver ever brought him to a spiritual view. His highest conception seemed simple practical convenience, such as an animal might appreciate—and in practice this holds for most people. If I proposed an improvement in his life, he simply said, without regret, that it was too late. Yet he thoroughly believed in honesty and similar virtues.

Still, a definite originality, however slight, appeared in him. Occasionally I saw him thinking for himself and expressing his own opinion, a phenomenon rare enough that I would gladly walk ten miles any day to witness it. It amounted to originating many social institutions afresh. Although hesitant and perhaps unable to express himself clearly, he always had a worthwhile thought behind the words. Yet his thinking remained so primitive and absorbed in bodily life that, though more promising than a merely learned person’s, it seldom ripened into anything reportable. He suggested that genius might exist in life’s lowest ranks, however permanently humble and unlettered: people always seeing for themselves, or never pretending to see at all, as bottomless as Walden Pond was believed to be, though perhaps dark and muddy.

Many travelers went out of their way to inspect me and my house, requesting water as an excuse. I explained that I drank from the pond, pointed toward it, and offered a dipper. Even my distance did not exempt me from the yearly visitation, around April 1, I think, when everyone moves about. I had my share of luck, though some visitors were curious specimens. Half-witted men came from the almshouse and elsewhere. I tried to exercise whatever intelligence they possessed and draw out their confessions, making intelligence itself our subject, which repaid me. Some proved wiser than the town’s supposedly far-seeing _overseers_ of the poor and its selectmen; I thought it time to reverse their positions. I learned there was little difference between half a wit and a whole one. One day a harmless, simple-minded pauper visited and said he wanted to live like me. I had often seen him and others employed as fencing: standing or sitting on bushel measures in fields to prevent both cattle and themselves from wandering. With utter simplicity and truth, beyond—or rather _below_—anything called humility, he told me he was “deficient in intellect.” Those were his words. The Lord had made him that way, but he supposed the Lord cared as much for him as anyone. “I have always been so,” he said, “from my childhood; I never had much mind; I was not like other children; I am weak in the head. It was the Lord’s will, I suppose.” There he stood, demonstrating his words’ truth. He presented a metaphysical puzzle. Seldom have I met someone on ground so promising: everything he said was so simple, sincere, and true. The more he seemed to humble himself, the more he was exalted. At first I wondered if this resulted from a wise policy. From that poor, weak-headed man’s foundation of truth and frankness, our conversation seemed capable of reaching something better than sages’ conversations.

Some guests were not ordinarily counted among the town’s poor, though they should have been; they certainly belonged among the world’s poor. They appealed not to hospitality but to _hospitalality_, wanting earnest help while announcing at the outset that they would never help themselves. I require a visitor not to be actually starving, though he may bring the finest appetite imaginable, however acquired. Recipients of charity are not guests. Some people never recognized the end of a visit, though I resumed work and answered from farther and farther away. In the migrating season, people of nearly every degree of intelligence arrived, some with more wits than they knew how to use. There were runaway slaves with plantation manners, occasionally listening like the fable’s fox as though hounds bayed on their trail, looking pleadingly at me as if to say:—
“O Christian, will you send me back?”

Among them was one actual fugitive slave whom I helped onward toward the north star.
